subsubtopic: SUGGESTION EMPLOYEES RECEIVE PAY CHEQUES BY MAIL- REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 on a matter which on the surface may not appear to be of urgent and pressing necessity but which recognizes that we are fast approaching the end of the month when pension cheques will be going out. The House is well aware of the firm belief of the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) in incentives within the work force as well as his commitment for increasing the efficiency of the Post Office. Since a great many businesses across Canada suffer from an interruption in the postal service, and since the lives of many Canadians, especially those depending on pension incomes, are frustrated by a disruption in the postal service, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday):
That the Postmaster General be instructed by this House to institute a policy whereby all postal employees will receive their pay cheques through the regular mail service using the postal code.

subsubtopic: AIR POLLUTION BY ASBESTOS FIBRES-SUGGESTED ADOPTION OF STANDARDS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to discuss a most urgent and important matter.
Because of the serious problems caused by asbestos fibre air pollution in the Thetford Mines area where, as early as 1949, at the time of the first strike in that sector, request was made to improve the situation but to no avail, and because of the serious problems created by data supplied by the CNTU and New York's Mount Sinai School of Medicine specialists, and all the more so because Thetford workers now on strike want their security guaranteed in this regard, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin):
That the House of Commons be allowed to discuss now this whole problem of asbestos fibre pollution, so that immediate steps can be taken in this regard, and that the federal Department of Environment assume as soon as possible its responsibility for setting up national standards by setting up a work schedule and the mechanism required to speed up the work of the research group in charge in the department.

subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-DECLARATION OF SALARIES OR FEES
speechtext: Any public servant appointed under the provisions of the Public Service Employment Act and employed in a department or agency for whom the Treasury Board represents the employer has no restrictions on other employment or outside activities except those specifically prohibited by legislation, such as certain types of political activity, provided that it would not (a) interfere with the employee's ability to satisfactorily discharge the duties for which he/she was employed, and (b) result in a potential or actual conflict of interest situation, and (c) result in bringing discredit to the public service. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PACIFIC REGION MANPOWER AND IMMIGRATION-CLUSTER MANAGEMENT CONCEPT
speechtext:
1. No additional positions are expected to result from the implementation of the cluster management concept by Pacific Region. The managers of the six CMCs designated as 'cluster headquarters' will be responsible for general supervision of the managers of those CMCs comprising their respective clusters. Whereas the five existing area managers are classified as PM-5, it is expected that cluster managers will be PM-6 when classification action

is completed and the managerial level of area manager is removed.
2.	In balance, it is expected that the increase in salary paid to (PM-6) cluster managers over that presently paid to the managers of those CMCs concerned, plus the salary of the district director, Yukon and the increase from PM-6 to SX-1 of the Vancouver metro manager (both of which are other aspects of Pacific Region's reorganization) will be more than compensated for by the elimination of the salaries of area managers. They were re-iterated in messages from the Minister of December 6, 1973 and April 11, 1974 to all staff. There are many factors which could influence the ultimate disposition of those cases where an incumbent area manager may not be the successful candidate for the cluster manager position in his present location. For example, he may succeed in obtaining the position of CMC manager in that or another location as our current general efforts to increase the base and broaden the range of CMC managers' classifications progress to fruition. Or he may win a competition for district director in another Region. Or some other factor of attrition, such as promotion or retirement of other staff members, may present a solution. In any event, the Minister's assurances shall continue to apply as the Department's reorganization and renewal program proceeds.

speechtext:
1. From 9 April 1974, when the provisions of the Foreign Investment Review Act that relate to acquisitions of control of Canadian business enterprises were proclaimed, until 7 March 1975, the Foreign Investment Review Agency issued certificates of receipt for 126 applications. The Agency has no authority to make decisions on applications under the Act. The Governor in Council allowed 52 applications, refused to allow 11 applications, and was deemed to have allowed 3 applications.
2. From 9 April 1974 to 7 March 1975, 16 certified applications were withdrawn by the applicant.
3 and 4. During the period under reference, an average of 100 days passed between the issue of a certificate of receipt for an application and the decision by the Governor in Council. This average covers both decisions to allow and decisions to refuse to allow. The Act provides that, before any decision can be made to refuse to allow, parties to the proposed transaction in question must be given the opportunity to make whatever further representations they wish. There is no statutory time limit on the period within which they may make those further representations.
5.	Applicants were advised of their right to make representations or further representations, under subsection 11(1), in relation to 83 applications between 9 April 1974 and 7 March 1975.
6.	As noted, the Agency makes no decisions itself on whether applications should be allowed or disallowed. Those decisions are made by the Governor in Council. Reasons for those decisions are given, by myself on behalf of the Government, whenever this can be done. See reply dated 26 February 1975 (Hansard page 3582). To date reasons for decisions to allow have been published in 32 cases out of a total of 52 allowed. From the outset the Government has recognized the need to avoid the disclosure of any information which could possibly jeopardize
Order Paper Questions
the legitimate interests of firms and individuals concerned. This is still the guiding principle, but experience has shown that it is possible to move towards wider disclosure than was the earlier practice without causing damage of that kind.
7.	The "working definition" used by the Government in determining whether there is significant benefit to Canada in any given proposal, and therefore whether it should be allowed or not, is that specified in the Foreign Investment Review Act. speechtext:
The fact of the matter is that the subject of Canada's position vis-a-vis commitments for grain shipments abroad has been raised on several occasions over the past few days. The serious concern of course comes not only from the point of view of employment but of our business internationally and this has been discussed in questions and answers. The work stoppages involved obviously represent a very difficult situation. It is difficult for the Chair, in reviewing the rules under Standing Order 26, to see how one could possibly look for a more serious matter and one which would be more qualified for debate under the provisions of that rule.
The only point of concern to the Chair is that the latter provisions of the Standing Order require that the Chair direct its attention to the possibility of the subject matter being discussed in some other reasonable way, and in that respect, since tomorrow is an allotted day under our Standing Orders, the hon. member, if he is in a position to ask the House to sit overtime, for a special debate, should be able to persuade his colleagues that the subject matter of his motion would be important enough to deserve priority with regard to the use of tomorrow's opposition day. However, that possibility of dealing with the matter has been removed as a result of the information given by the hon. member that he and his colleagues are not in a position of authority or control over that subject matter because of internal arrangements among the parties that are well known to all members of the House.
Accordingly, I see no reason why I should not accept the motion put forward by the hon. member, which conforms with the provisions of Standing Order 26. Therefore, I put the following questions to the House: has the hon. member leave to move the motion for the purpose of discussing the matter stated by him?

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my colleague the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) has indicated, we are opposed to the passage of the bill now before us and the incorporation of Petro-Can. We believe there must be a halt to the continued growth of government in Canada. The weight of government grows-in fact to the point that it is now estimated that one in seven of our work force is employed by the government.
In March, 1925, when figures were first published, federal government employees numbered 39,000, compared with
121,000	in March, 1946, the beginning of the post-war period. There are now 443,192 people in the federal employ. It may be relevant to point out that in 1925 there was one federal government employee for every 238 Canadians. In 1946, the ratio was down to one in 102, and now the ratio is one in 50; that is, there is one federal government employee for every 50 men, women and children in this country. With today's automation, one naturally would have assumed that this ratio would have been somewhat reversed.
The cost of running governments, particularly the federal government, has risen at an alarming rate. In 1967, the end of our first 100 years, the federal budget was approximately $10 billion and today it is more than triple that amount. Expenditures must be covered by revenue, and total government revenue expressed as a percentage of gross national product has risen from 16.8 per cent in 1926 to 30.4 per cent in 1946, the last of the war years. In 1958,

that figure had dropped to 25.5 per cent. Today, however, 38.2 per cent of the total gross national product accrues to the government in the form of revenue.
If this trend continues, it will, in my opinion, place an unbearable load on the productive sectors of this economy, bearing in mind that it is the private sector which is geared to efficiency. I think it can generally be said that within business it is widely felt that a dollar saved is a dollar earned. In government, however, we find the philosophy is a dollar not spent is a dollar lost from next year's estimates.
We in the official opposition believe that the public sector must be limited in its invasion into the private sector. It was rather startling to hear our Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) say today, in respect of the Canada Development Corporation which was incorporated on the strict understanding that 90 per cent of its stock would be turned over to individuals or institutions in Canada, that to date no arrangements have been made to sell even one share of that Crown corporation, and that in fact it is likely that the underwriters involved have refused to sell any of the corporation's stock.
Yesterday evening I was reviewing the record of some of our Crown corporations and I pointed out that if parliament is foolish enough to go ahead with the incorporation of Petro-Can, it will be the sixtieth Crown corporation to be owned by the federal government. I could also have pointed out that while there are 60 Crown corporations, there are in existence approximately 120 subsidiaries of those corporations. So approximately 180 legal entities are operating under the ownership of the federal government.
Before we plunge into the incorporation of this new entity for which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) is hankering, surely it would be only prudent for every member of this House to consider what has transpired to date in respect of federal government enterprises. In this regard I would refer hon. members to page 271 of The National Finances for 1974-75. There they will find that the total assets of federal government enterprises are listed at $17.3 billion for the year ended December 31, 1972. At that time, the net worth held in those corporations by the federal government on behalf of all Canadians was $3.4 billion. But here is the real grabber: when we look at the profit and loss picture of these corporations we find that over the last few years, in spite of the fact that the federal government has $3.4 billion invested, they have been run at an over-all loss. In one year, 1972, the year for which the most recent figures are available, they earned a total of only $25 million on a net worth investment of $3.4 billion-less than 1 per cent.
With that type of background, I ask the backbench members of the Liberal Party why they are so anxious to push this bill through the House. I would like them to show good faith with the Canadian public by offering to invest $1,000 each in Petro-Can and put their money where their vote and their mouth is. I think you would find a very different attitude if Liberal backbenchers were asked to contribute $1,000 each to a concept like Petro-Can. Then we would find the true facts. They must know that this will be a losing proposition, yet they totally ignore the
Pet ro-Canada
trust that has been given to them to sit in this parliament and invest public moneys prudently.
I should like to review some of the other situations which pertain in respect of these Crown corporations. Last evening I referred to the CBC. I suggested that when one looks at the statements of the CBC it would be refreshing to consider similar statements of the private television networks in the United States and Canada and compare their expenditure ratios and the profit and loss picture. If we look at ABC, NBC and CBS in the United States, we find that those three companies, in relation to their broadcasting activities alone, make more money than the total loss of the CBC.
Let me put it another way: the CBC lost almost as much in the year 1973 as those three companies earned. Surely, as the senior parliament of this country, we must start asking why. Is it proper use of Canadian taxpayers' money when there is a loss, in the case of the CBC, of over $200 million in one year?
In the last decade there has been a change from public to more private initiative in many of the socialist nations of the world, while many of the western industrialized nations-including Canada under the Trudeau, Liberal government-have been following the reverse course. I would suggest that lately among academics and bureaucrats in the west there has been an almost unquestioned presumption in favour of public participation and something approaching hostility to private initiative.
Prior to the First World War western attitudes saw business in a different light. It was agreed that business was then the centre of the economic world and government tended to be incidental. Today, governments no longer operate in a business-centred environment; it is a social-centred environment with which they are concerned. This is where I believe confusion has arisen in the past 30 years between the people and the governments of the western nations, including Canada. In their anxiety to relieve social needs, governments have continually and needlessly infringed on the private sector; they have responded to current problems on an ad hoc basis with little reference to longer range considerations. This develops an uncertain economic climate within which it is difficult for businessmen to operate.
Since 1939, government expenditures in Canada have risen from a total of less than $1 billion, or 16 per cent of the gross national product, to $45 billion, or 38 per cent of the GNP in 1973. In the current year it is estimated that the government "take" will be about 40 per cent.
Governmental activity in Canada falls into three broad categories. The first is the traditional role of surveillance, protection and regulation on behalf of Canadian citizens. This would include, for example, the setting of monetary and fiscal policies and the application of regulations where there are natural monopolies in the country. A second field is the transfer of income by government from region to region or from person to person. A third activity is the direct participation in the production of our resources, the manufacture of goods, the providing of commercial services and the operation of business generally.

Petro-Canada
In today's social-centred environment it is important that both the private and public sectors distinguish these three categories of governmental functions and understand them. In my opinion, governmental activity should be confined mainly to the traditional role of surveillance, protection and regulation. They have a limited but desirable role to play in category two, the transfer of income, but they should avoid like the plague extended participation in the third field of commercial activity such as Petro-Can. In recent years, however, an overwhelming increase of government spending as a proportion of gross national product has been in government current expenditures on goods and services and in transfer payments to persons.
Prior to 1950, government current expenditure for goods and services was relatively static at approximately 10 per cent of our gross national product. By 1973, government current purchases of goods and services had risen to $22.8 billion, or 19.2 per cent of the gross national product- almost twice as much as its share of the gross national product in the year 1950. In 1929, transfer payments to persons represented 1.5 per cent of the gross national product. By 1973, such transfer payments to persons had risen to $11.2 billion, or about 9.5 per cent of the gross national product. The federal government has been the major innovator in this field of income maintenance and stabilization.
Recent growth in federal government operational activities is also reflected in the government's loans to and investments in Crown corporations to which I have referred. These corporations between 1968 and 1974 more than doubled in size. The government has advanced some $16 billion to these corporations, and at the present time
140,000	Canadians are employed by Crown corporations in this nation.
Sharply higher governmental expenditures for goods and services and transfer payments to persons to equalize incomes required government revenues also to jump from 21 per cent of the gross national product in 1938 to 38 per cent in 1973. About 12.5 per cent of this increase-that is, of the 17 per cent-was accounted for by a sharp rise in direct personal taxes including other transfers from persons. I believe that is what we often forget in this House.
The person who is actually paying for the recklessness of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) and his colleagues is the individual taxpayer in Canada. It is not the fat cat, it is not the big something or other that they like to conjure up; it is the average person in this country who will have to pay for the minister's folly. That is why I would like to re-emphasize that if the Liberal members are confident that this will be a worth-while venture, let them each put $1,000 on the line; let them go to the minister and say they will put up $1,000 to invest in his fine idea, namely, Petro-Can. I bet there would not be 5 per cent of them making such an investment.
Direct personal taxes, including other tranfers from persons, now account for about 40 per cent of all revenues raised by governments, compared with 13 per cent in 1938. That is a jump of over 300 per cent in the total revenue

ratio of the federal government from the personal sector alone. These shifts in the source of tax revenue lead to the conclusion that continued increases in government spending for goods and services and the expansion of transfer payments will, in my view, dull the personal initiatives of those Canadians who are required to pay these sharply increased taxes.
In September of 1969, the Economic Council of Canada issued a review which they entitled "Perspective 1975" in which they said at page 26:
Governments will be absorbing or redistributing about 37 per cent of the nation's total income by 1975 compared with 33 per cent in 1967.
Then they added the following:
One of the most important implications of our estimates is that major new government spending programs requiring large additional resources can only be accommodated through large cutbacks in existing programs.
This is an objective that they point out is in itself highly desirable. Then they add that if those alternatives are not chosen, the additional revenue must be raised-
-through tax increases leading to a larger shift of resources than we have indicated from the private-mainly the consumer-sector to the government sector of the economy.
With the government "take" already at 38 per cent of our gross national product two years before 1975, and with taxes at an all-time high, those concerned-namely, the Trudeau government-have obviously taken the third course and opted to increase taxes rather than cut back existing programs or increase efficiency as suggested by the Economic Council of Canada.
In my opinion, the Canadian government has not acted responsibly in the past decade in administering their trust on behalf of the Canadian people under category one, especially with respect to the fiscal and monetary increases of over 20 per cent per year which have been dictated, I suggest, by political expediency rather than sound economic reasoning. As a result, inflation has been three times higher in this country than the Economic Council of Canada predicted it would be as recently as 1969.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) "let it all hang out" a week ago today when he testified before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. In answer to the question, "Why have you allowed government spending to grow so quickly?" he said:
In democracies today, there are no such things as economic cycles; there are political cycles, depending on the pressures of public policy and depending on the parliamentary or congressional process at the time. One may tend to see this operating now in the United States where you have a Republican President and a Democratic Congress. Certainly we were under political imperatives-
He was referring to the last parliament.
-where the pressures were stronger in a minority rather than a majority parliament. Those happen to be facts of life.
At that point I interjected, "You wanted to be re-elected", and the minister replied, "Those happen to be facts of life". Unfortunately for the Canadian people, this government put their re-election ahead of handling our economy in a responsible way. If you look at the charts, you can see exactly when this government determined they would call the July 8 election last year. The money increase shows it very clearly. It was going up sharply at over 20 per cent

per year until the spring of last year, and then it plateaud very dramatically to a negative growth which Dr. Ray-nauld, chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, later described as excessively restrictive. In short, they blew up the economy in anticipation of the July 8 election, and then in order to counter the excess that they had deliberately put into the economy they contracted it unduly. That is one of the reasons we have 839,000 people out of work today.
The Minister of Finance apparently does not know now which way to turn to adjust his economic stance. With such an attitude adopted by our Minister of Finance, is it any wonder that we have today's mish-mash of economic inconsistencies, high inflation, high unemployment and current account trade deficits of an admitted $3 billion and, according to the Minister of Finance yesterday, they could be as high as $5 billion?
Let me put it another way. With the Post Office losing over $100 million a year and still not able to deliver the mail on time, with our airports losing still more and never being open for certain, and with our harbours-a subject which will be debated tonight-struck regularly by a public service that was given the right to strike by this government or its predecessor in 1967, is it rational for some, including government members, to suggest that Petro-Can should be incorporated to give the government still more operations to run?
Let there be no mistake; it is no accident that fully planned economies in the world are run by dictators. You cannot create or preserve prosperity in a fully planned economy through a democratic form of government; they do not mix. A marketplace economy which preserves private initiative will produce the greatest wealth for the greatest number of people. A competitive private enterprise system is not only an economically efficient institution but it also safeguards individual liberty.
Let me deal with these two facts separately. First, let us consider the economic efficiency of the private enterprise system. As a business person new to the political arena in Ottawa, I am astounded by the inefficient, disorganized, non-productive government activities I witness every day. Time and again, when one would hope the government would act in a businesslike manner in settling strikes or in extending assistance to commercial concerns one finds they are swayed by political considerations. Government does not have the discipline found in private business. To survive in business you must make a profit or at least break even. Not so in government. In private business a dollar saved is a dollar earned. Unfortunately, in public business a dollar not spent is a dollar lost from next year's estimates. The net effect of this is reflected in the Crown corporation statements to which I have referred: in short, a net worth investment on the part of the federal government of $3.4 billion, in 1972, and a return on that investment of $25 million, which is less than 1 per cent. Given the chance, who among the Liberal backbenchers or cabinet ministers would want to invest in that type of portfolio?
Let me be more specific. An interesting comparison can be drawn between Central Mortgage and Housing Corpo-
Petro-Canada
ration in Canada and the Federal National Mortgage Association in the United States. Both companies were organized for similar functions; both were owned by their respective governments up to 1968. In that year, the Federal National Mortgage Association-known affectionately at Fannie Mae-was turned over, in a unique plan, to the private sector with the United States government retaining a supervisory role. The contrast between the two companies from that date is startling. In 1967, CMHC had assets of $3.6 billion, while Fannie Mae had assets of $5.4 billion. That year, CMHC earned $7.2 million, while Fannie Mae's net income was $15.4 million. By 1973, the assets of CMHC grew to $6.6 billion but its net income went down to $2.9 million. Fannie Mae, on the other hand, by 1973 had $24.3 billion in assets and its net income had risen to $125.7 million, after having contributed $106 million in federal taxes to the United States.

They got their money back much faster, and in its entirety, than the taxpayers of Canada will get theirs out of Petro-Canada. A competitive private enterprise system will out-perform publicly-run institutions, and rather than being a drain on the economy it will contribute substantial tax revenues to it. Let me deal with the second reason I believe a competitive private enterprise system is preferable to government intervention at the operational level. A competitive private enterprise system safeguards individual liberty. Milton Friedman stated in 1962:
The kind of economic organization that provides economic freedom directly, namely, competitive capitalism, also promotes political freedom because it separates economic power from political power and in this way enables the one to offset the other.
Competitive markets, according to Friedman-
-reduce greatly the range of issues that must be decided through political means, and thereby to minimize the extent to which government need participate directly in the game. The characteristic feature of action through political channels is that it tends to require or enforce substantial conformity. The great advantage of the market, on the other hand, is that it permits wide diversity.
Yet this same competitive private enterprise system that extends economic freedom acts also to promote political freedom. For the fundamental threat to freedom is the power to coerce, be it in the hands of a monarch, a dictator, an oligarch, or a momentary majority.
I suggest a momentary majority such as we have under the Trudeau government. Mr. Friedman went on to say:
The preservation of freedom requires the elimination of such concentration of power to the fullest possible extent and the dispersal and distribution of whatever power cannot be eliminated through a system of checks and balances. By removing the organization of economic activity from the central political authority, the market eliminates this source of coercive power. It enables economic strength to be a check to political power rather than a reinforcement.
If governments continue to enter category number three-that is, the operational business field-they will

tend to lower efficiency through the making of political rather than businesslike decisions. As a nation becomes more frustrated with this inefficient approach and resulting strikes, there is a distinct possibility the voters will turn to a strong man be he of the right or the left: He need only promise some type of order and some type of security to win favour.
Let us not forget, when we are considering the extension of the public domain, Mr. Speaker, that history has shown that man treasures order and security even more than he does freedom. That is why I believe we must resist, with all the determination we can muster, the empire-building exploit that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is about to embark upon with Petro-Can. Petro-Can is not going to make the oil industry more competitive. Tommyrot! It is not going to find oil that would not have been found anyway. The fact is, it is going to be a tremendous drain on the taxpayer.

Others might say that the shortages were a false alarm, that the industry would have provided our needs and that the government did not need to go into the market itself. Anyway, they might say, the government paid too much for what it purchased in that panic situation.
What would this new national oil company do for us other than provide some executive jobs in still another government bureaucracy? I should like to look for a moment at the stated purposes of the corporation as set out in clause 3 of the bill. I will not read the whole clause, but it reads in part:
-to establish within the energy industries in Canada ... and to engage in exploration for, and the production, distribution, refining and marketing of, fuels.
The extent of the purposes set out in that small clause leaves no room to doubt what the government intends to do to the industry in this country. It sounds as though they will have adequate powers. Clause 6 sets out the details of the powers and duties of the corporation. We see that they are entitled to engage in exploration, research and development, to "import, produce, transport, distribute, refine and market," and to "produce, distribute, transport and market other fuels and energy". I emphasize the word "other", Mr. Speaker. Clause 6(e) empowers it-
-to engage or invest in ventures or enterprises related to the exploration, production, importation, distribution, refining and marketing of fuel, energy and related resources.
From those key words it is apparent that this government would like to give itself power to get involved in the whole fuel industry. I cannot think of a single aspect of the fuel industry that has been left out of the objects, powers and duties as set out in that clause. If there were any question about powers that were missing, they are described in clause 7 which, referring to powers alone, reads:
The corporation may do such things as it deems expedient for or conducive to the furtherance of the objects of the corporation, within and outside Canada, and, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, the corporation may-
Then it lists 26 additional powers, which I shall not read. I am thankful that our alphabet only runs to 26 characters, Mr. Speaker, when I think of what they would have done if they had tried to go from beginning to end of some of
Petro-Canada
the longer alphabets in the world. From the wording, which gives the corporation the authority to do all things which are incidental and conducive to the attainment of its objectives and powers, there is little doubt as to what the government has in mind. As the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) said, this will truly be a glorious government conglomerate, but will it pay taxes even if it does put taxpaying enterprisers out of business? I should like to remind hon. members that the enterprise system pays taxes of all sorts, and in huge amounts, to all kinds and levels of government. Some of my friends have overlooked this fact and I like to remind them of these things.
I do not know why we should not doubt Petro-Can's ability to pay taxes. Let us consider the operations of the CNR to which the hon. member for York-Simcoe alluded. According to the annual report for 1973-the 1974 report is not yet available-the CNR, that large, government conglomerate, is involved with 41 separate companies which engage in many different businesses. But does the CNR pay taxes? No, it does not.
Rail transport is important for this country and some contend that private enterprisers might not provide adequate rail service. But what about the Canadian National hotel operation? Canadian National hotels compete with hotels run by private enterprisers which make profits. According to page 11 of the annual report, CN hotel operations had a net income of $4 million. That is only part of the story. If you want the full story you must turn to page 34 of the annual report, where you will find the consolidated income statement for the year ended December 31. The statement shows that after deducting all expenses except one, the CNR had a net income of $48 million.
The last item reveals the full story as it shows the total interest on debt. Any businessman can tell you that interest payments are a substantial factor in any business operation. Unless you consider how much interest you pay, you cannot determine your net income. On page 35 of the annual report, under "Source and application of funds for the year ended December 31," the CNR is forced to admit that it obtained its funds from the government, as the second line in the first item reads, "Government of Canada in respect of deficit for the year." The upshot is that the Canadian National ran a deficit on operations of over $21 million.
We cannot tell how much of this loss is directly attributable to hotels and how much is directly attributable to the railway operation or to the operation of any of the other 39 companies involved with CN. The government makes good these losses by taxing other hotel owners who operate their hotels profitably. This government practice led some thinker of the Pacific Trollers Association to define capital punishment in a new way. He said that capital punishment is when the government taxes you to get capital so that it can go into competition with you, and then taxes the profits on your business in order to pay its losses. What a sad commentary on what is going on!
Let us look at another government fiasco, Connaught Laboratories. Connaught Laboratories was a well respected operation of the University of Toronto. It provided

March 19, 1975
Petro-Canada
high-quality products at reasonable prices. Then along came the CDC and acquired Connaught Laboratories. Since then what has happened to Connaught Laboratories? It has run up huge operating losses and produced products of questionable quality. This may result in damage awards against the company or, shall we say, against the government. We might as well say they will be awarded against the taxpayer, because he will pay in the end.
Let me list some other Crown corporations or some other fiascos which have resulted from the government's entering the sphere of private enterprise. There is the CBC, about which I will not go into detail, and Air Canada. The list is not endless as I understand that only 59 Crown corporations use-I do not say "consume"- some $16 billion of taxpayers' money. I have asked if Petro-Can is necessary. I ask, are many of our Crown corporations necessary? Certainly there are fields in which the government must be involved, but need it be involved in the broadcasting business?
The CBC has run up tremendous losses, as my friend from York-Simcoe suggested. There is no need for the government to be in the broadcasting business and run up these losses, which absorb I don't know how many hundreds of millions of dollars, because private enterprisers would be only too glad to take over the operation of the CBC. Air Canada, as a Crown corporation, may have been needed in the 1930s during the birth of the air travel explosion, but today many airlines are operated by private enterprisers and they do not need government help. Air Canada, as a Crown corporation, does a bad job and ends up by being a burden on the taxpayer instead of contributing to the economy of this country, which is what the airline would do if private enterprise were running it.
Some hon. members may say, "If you let private enterprise run the airline, you will not see proper service in the outlying areas of the country." To answer them I refer to the telephone industry. In my province of British Columbia private enterprise runs the telephone service, and the most remote community in British Columbia is served. The reason is simple: although it costs the telephone company money to service remote communities, it is told that such service is a condition of its licence. If it wants to provide telephone service in Vancouver, it must supply similar telephone service in far-out communities. That simple solution could be applied by the government to other areas.
Private enterprisers expect problems when dealing with the government. The new president of the British Columbia and Yukon Chamber of Commerce summed it up this way, as reported in the Globe and Mail of February 20, 1975:
Dealing with the government has been a real education to some of us. And I think the basic reason is that most of us in mining are technically trained, we have training which deals with facts and logic, and we were going up against a government philosophy.
And you soon find that facts and reason just don't apply against that. They don't make a dent. It took a while for us to appreciate that... But they must leave enough to provide an incentive to the industry and they're not doing that.
Other colleagues have expressed that sentiment. Unless the government provides the free enterprisers of the coun-

try with incentive, our system as we know it in Canada today will not survive.
Government expenses are continually rising, with the help of the 59 Crown corporations I mentioned and with the help of an ever increasing bureaucracy. Is our large bureaucracy really necessary? I think we should compare our situation with that of the state of California. The Governor of the state, on taking office some eight years ago, observed that nothing is more opposed to creativeness than bureaucracy. We should bear that in mind when debating this bill.
I hope hon. members will bear the following facts in mind: California entered 1975 with a constantly decreasing welfare population receiving constantly increasing benefits, with financially and technically sound energy and water supply systems-and we do not even have an energy policy in this country-and with enforced environmental standards that are both lowering air and water pollution and preserving an extraordinary range of recreational opportunities. The state of California has established a superb highway system that has become an orderly segment of an integrated transportation system. I am sorry the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) is not present to hear what can be done. I think the key to the situation in California is this: in 1975 the state employs no more people than it employed eight years ago, even though in eight years state spending has doubled and state services have multiplied. One cannot make similar claims for the operations of this government.
I should like to compare the California situation with a similar sample in my part of the country, the province of British Columbia, where of course we have an NDP government. Out there a nice backbencher by the name of Mr. Nunweiler came from the interior of British Columbia, Prince George, and for some reason or other it was decided that Mr. Nunweiler should be a minister. There was not a portfolio available for him, so he was made a minister without portfolio. That probably satisfied him and also his constituents, so instead of being a lowly backbencher at a mere $24,000 per annum salary, he is now a cabinet minister with a salary of $45,000. Of course, after that he had to have an executive assistant, a full-time secretary and two clerk-stenographers. This amounted to an additional expenditure of $50,000 for his office.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: You get that in Tory Ontario.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Then he had to have an office in Prince George-after all, that is his home town-and the office in Prince George had to be staffed as well. So he employs an executive assistant, an economic planning consultant, a social policy co-ordinator, a public liaison officer, a resource planning consultant and an administrative assistant. When you add up all those salaries it comes to another $94,000.
In addition, of course, there are office expenses amounting to $25,000, travelling expenses of $40,000, and office furniture in the amount of $10,000. Then there is the cost of printing and publishing-necessary if anyone is to believe us-and printing and publication costs amount to $25,000, as well as advertising, just in case anybody forgets

who that minister is, costing another $5,000. Then, taking a leaf out of the book of the government in Ottawa, there is a final item-consultant fees and expenses, $50,000 for the year. Mr. Speaker, when you add all that up, instead of having a nice backbencher at a cost of $24,000 we have a minister without portfolio with expenditures totalling $402,000 for the year.
It will be said that all the rules are clearly set out in Bill C-8 and that there is no danger of what I am suggesting taking place. Let us ask ourselves how Ottawa has been doing in this area, then, in its other legislation. Only a few cases involving the 1972 income tax reforms have yet come before the courts of this country, yet judges are already showing their frustration with the sloppy drafting of the legislation. They have been coming down hard on the side of the taxpayers even when this has gone against the apparent intent of the law. I emphasize here the words "apparent intent" because, as will be understood from my remarks, the judges do not even know what parliament intended to do. There was a recent series of cases which the courts feel may be just the start of a flood of litigation. The judges have indicated that the tax rules may be unenforceable if the wording is too vague, complex or obscure to understand. One judge had this to say:
I cannot know for a fact what parliament in its wisdom meant by the inclusion of the word "active"-But I think I can assume that to the legislators it meant something, or the word would not have been inserted.
This judge said later, in giving judgment:
I am also just as certain, if one can be certain of anything about this section ... that it was never intended, in my view, to cover a company such as this.
He ruled in favour of the company and said that his decision was based solely on the way in which the section had been worded. What a testimony from one of the keepers of justice in this country, to make comments of that kind about legislation put forward by the government! I am afraid that with the government's record in connection with this type of legislation, Bill C-8 may turn out to be worse than even we think it might.
I would like to give one more piece of personal experience which tends to show the ineptness of the government when it comes to legislation. Just this month I received in Vancouver, addressed to my business office there, a letter mailed from Montreal on the letterhead of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs addressing me as a professional closely involved with corporation and suggesting that I would be concerned with the Canada Business Corporations Act. The following is a paragraph of that letter, Mr. Speaker:
Consumer and Corporate Affairs is designing a comprehensive seminar on the Canada Business Corporations Act.
They know we will not be able to understand it the way it is written, so they want us to come out and be told how it is going to work. Then they cannot quite decide what they want to do, so the letter goes on:
When do you want it? Where? What would you like to discuss?
Of course, the simple answer which the government to this day seems to ignore constantly is that all we want is to be able to understand the laws. As I said a moment ago, we have absolutely no assurance that Bill C-8 is going to
Petro-Canada
be any better than the laws the government has been passing recently.
When a government department or corporation gets loose, it is time for us to look out. For example, I would like to refer to something being done by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation: it will show how tight their policies are. In 1973, CMHC spent $12,500,000 to acquire an industrial estate known as Granville Island in Vancouver. Then in 1974 it had to spend $1 million on redevelopment, administration and operation of this industrial estate. Now we are getting into the 1975-76 estimates, and they include $7.75 million for this project. This may seem like a worth-while project and I am sure it will bring satisfaction to many Vancouver residents even though it is located under a high bridge and is unseen by all but a few.
I really think it is time, in this day of energy conservation and transportation difficulties, that the idea of relocating all industries which were on this industrial estate to the suburbs should be looked at as well. All the people who live in the centre part of town and who would have liked to work in this estate are now faced with commuting to the suburbs. It certainly seems a bit backward to me. But there is not the slightest intention of providing any housing on Granville Island and there certainly are no mortgages involved. So my question-one which I have asked the minister before now-is: what is Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation doing in this venture? The only explanation I can think of is that the government got caught up with the original falsehood of Granville Island itself, because Granville Island is not even an island.
Mr. Speaker, the former auditor general, Maxwell Henderson, summed it up last week when he said the erosion of parliament's control over government spending continues. In the past ten years, spending has increased fivefold and now the estimates are $28 billion. I have often accused the government of being the chief contributor to inflation in this country. Of course, there is imported inflation, but the present government ignores the total problem or, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says, they will wrestle it to the ground; and the government hopes for the best.
Finally, last week the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) admitted that cost increases from wage settlements were disturbing and that they could be dangerous to Canada. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that through the examples I have cited the House may realize that the good intention which undoubtedly the minister had when he sponsored Bill C-8 will be no match for the forces which will come into play after it is made law. We would be well advised to reconsider carefully the function of the government in the enterprise system before we get swallowed up in another monstrous, uncontrollable bureaucracy. Just as the sorcerer's apprentice became the slave of the broomsticks because after starting them up with the best of intentions he found he had lost control of the situation, Canada will have lost control of the situation, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I make a few comments on this matter I wonder whether it is a coincidence that since 1968 the Liberal government has created twice as many Crown corporations and, if we include the 1975-76 budget, has also dou-

Petro-Canada
bled its spending. I suppose it would be reasonable to think that with this creation of Crown corporations and the government's embarking upon business ventures, there should be an easing of government spending. That is to say, by taking over some of the services Canadians demand which were previously carried on by private enterprise profitably, the government should be able to make a profit which could then be applied to the public purse to defray some of the expenses of government in carrying out these services.
Having been in private business, I always dreamt that some day I would be able to start and run a business where I had no worries about lack of working capital. I dreamt I would be able to walk into a bank and tell them what I wanted to do: I would say to them; "I think this is a great dream; there is no way it can fail". Every businessman starts out in business with this vision. The banker would say to me; "Now, don't worry about it, Frank; you go ahead. There is no bottom to the barrel, so don't worry about your working capital; away you go".
I also dreamt that some day I would run a business where I would not have to go to the bank at all; I would not have to pay any taxes; I would pay no interest on my working capital; I would pay no royalties if things got tough: indeed, I would pay none of the taxes or charges private businessmen have to pay today.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: What a dream!

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Yes, what a dream! I never realized that I would have to get elected to parliament before I could become a director, so to speak, in one huge corporation that has no problem with finding money, a corporation that dips into a barrel that has no bottom, that does not have to charge itself any taxes. In a pinch, it can write off royalties. What a way to run a business! We all know, Mr. Speaker, that many of the businesses this government runs show no profit even though they pay no interest on their borrowings and pay no royalties. They are bailed out repeatedly every year. All they have to do is to dip into the barrel and take out millions of dollars.
Some of the Crown corporations to which I refer are disgusting and disgraceful. Surely to goodness the government's purpose is to equalize wealth and opportunity in this country. I go further and say that government has the responsibility to provide essential public and social services such as hospitals, schools, law an order. I do not have to tell my colleagues what the original purpose of government was supposed to be, because they all know. But is it the purpose of government to involve itself in transportation, housing, communications-all the many headaches the government has that are also headaches to the taxpayer? The Canadian taxpayer is no longer a taxpayer; he is a shareholder in a huge non-profit corporation.
What is a non-profit corporation, particularly in a country like ours? Any corporation that does not make a profit at the end of the year does not, of course, have any resources or money left to expand. At a time when we realize the necessity for agriculture to increase its productive capacity, and there is a challenge to create secondary industry throughout Canada to protect us against the sell-out of our resources, the government is taking over more and more services and not making a profit. This

means there will be no expansion, because the government has no money left at the end of the year to expand these services.
The bill we are discussing today is proposing to incorporate a company called Petro-Canada. The minister has told us that one of the reasons for Petro-Can is to enable the government to participate in Syncrude. I did not have an opportunity of talking about Syncrude previously, so let me illustrate what I think is happening to the shareholders, the taxpayers, in the Syncrude venture. I will have to take the minister's word for it when he says that the reason the federal government is getting into the Syncrude venture is to assure Canadians a steady supply of petroleum resources. This is all very laudable; but he is going to spend $300 million, first of all. He will have to go into partnership with corporations which have been identified in this House as irresponsible and as rip-off artists. Did the minister have to go into this venture with an investment of $300 million, which put him in a minority position, just to assure security of supply of petroleum resources for Canadians?
The fact is that 40 per cent of our fossil fuels in Canada are not in crude oil or natural gas, but in coal. It is also a fact that the United States has not only recognized the worth of coal but has also recognized it is much cheaper to develop the process of coal gasification and coal liquefaction, and to assure themselves of security of supply in that way, than it is to go into the Syncrude project.
As a practical businessman, I look at Syncrude in this way: it is a great project for the province of Alberta; it has created a lot of activity in the province and I congratulate the Premier of Alberta because he made a smart move, particularly since somebody else pays the bill. We all know the cost of a barrel of oil today, but the cost of a barrel of oil when this project is finally realized will be at least $12. We also know the margins that the OPEC countries enjoy so far as their export price of crude oil is concerned. In my opinion, there is no way that the OPEC countries will diminish their exports of crude oil once Syncrude comes on stream. They will continue to sell it as they always have and in order to do so they will simply lower the price by $3 or $4 a barrel. They could even lower the price by $6 in order to stay in a competitive position with Syncrude. That is one practical point that I want to bring out.
Another point I want to make is this. No one can tell me that people in Montreal and Toronto are voluntarily going to pay an artificially high price just to keep alive a brainwave that the Premier of Alberta might have had regarding investment in Canada. Therefore, all that Syncrude will do for Canada is to assure us of a continued flow of energy supply at a cost that we will not be able to afford, and we will continue to buy oil from Venezuela and the other OPEC countries.
For $300 million we are, as taxpayers, now partners or shareholders in a venture with large oil companies which will, when the facts are all known, pull out of this venture and write off their loses against other income, leaving us with the whole $2 billion project which will really never get off the ground.

In almost everything we do, we follow the United States, but this government is not following the leadership of that country in assuring us of a supply of energy for the future. If it were following that leadership it would embark upon some ambitious and intelligent research into new sources of energy such as hydrogen from seawater or other exotic sources about which we have heard.
I am not bothered so much about the fact that this government intends to embark upon a venture the purpose of which is to establish within the energy industries in Canada a Crown-owned company with authority to explore for hydrocarbon deposits. That does not worry me so much even though there is only one chance in 50, as demonstrated by private industry lately, of success in finding significant deposits of oil and natural gas in the areas that have been explored in the last five years. Can you imagine Canadian taxpayers being asked to take one chance in 50 in a business venture with their money? These are the same taxpayers who provide not 40 per cent, as my colleague said earlier, but closer to 50 per cent of total government revenue. These are the same taxpayers who have a very difficult time to provide the most essential public services and properly nutritious food for their children. These taxpayers are being asked to go into this kind of venture, but that is not what worries me most: what does worry me most is the last line of this paragraph which outlines the purpose of the proposed act as follows:
-to carry out research and development projects in relation to hydrocarbons and other fuels-
I am happy with that because, as I have said, that should take place. But it continues:
-and to engage in exploration for, and the production, distribution, refining and marketing of, fuels.
This is the crux of the matter. As far as energy, petroleum resources, fossil fuels and minerals are concerned, this government has gone all the way. Private enterprise has run its course, because the government can go out, run the corner service station and make the final contract with the customer, if we pass this bill.
In this country we are rushing toward socialism and communism faster than the communist countries are in competing to enter the enterprise and incentive systems. We are heading in a direction that is opposite to the most popular one in the world today. What worries me is that private enterprise is being made to pay taxes to provide various governments in this country with sufficient funds to be transferred to other provinces. These funds are being channelled into businesses which will compete with those which generated the funds in the first place. The transfer payments which are made from the western provinces, Ontario and others are channelled into these giant, nonprofit organizations.
I had an experience the other day in the province of British Columbia which of course has been a socialist province for the last three years. I travel a lot and have to eat in restaurants and I worry a bit about reports I read regarding bad hamburger meat, and so on. As a precaution, I take a little medicine once in a while to offset this. The medicine I like is made by Seagram's. I walked into one of the people's stores in British Columbia, the government liquor store, and asked for a bottle of my favourite brand.
Petro-Canada
The clerk told me I could not have a bottle of that brand because it was hot. I am a little naive about these things, as I suppose all of us are, and I told him there was really nothing wrong with hot whisky as long as you had a twist of lemon and a little water with it. I told him I would buy a bottle anyway, whether it was hot or not. He explained to me that it was not the heat of the whisky that bothered him, but the fact that the people in the distillery were involved in a squabble over the equity of profit transfer in the company. Apparently the employees in the government liquor store had decided to take the side of the distillery employees and they would not sell any more of that distillery's products, so there would be no more profits and all the problems would be solved.
I cannot view this as anything but an intervention by government in a labour dispute. These employees have entered this dispute by deciding that the employees of the distillery were right and that the distillery was not treating its employees properly, and as a result will not sell any more of its products. I can see this happening in other areas where the government is involved in business. It will be much easier for the government to solve some of the labour disputes that may arise in the future. Let us consider how some of these Crown corporations are making out with their labour problems, particularly those corporations we expect to provide essential public services. Let us take the Post Office as an example. We do not have to point out the performance of the Post Office in the last few years or at this particular time.
Let us also consider transportation facilities and the grain handlers on the west coast. The last time we talked about settling a strike on the west coast, the government took sides. Socialist governments in particular always take the side of labour in settling these disputes. At that time the government imposed a settlement on the grain companies on the west coast with which they found it hard to live. It was found that many of the employees who were members of the Public Service Alliance, those at the port of Vancouver but more particularly at the port of Prince Rupert, were getting about 25 per cent less than people working for private companies.
At the time we all warned the minister that unless we found a solution to the problem that was facing government employees on the west coast, the settlement of the strike at that time would only be a partial solution. We were right, and we are experiencing another strike on the west coast. Incidentally, there are six more unions to commence labour negotiations within the next six months to a year. If we achieve a settlement of the strike by the grain handlers and the Public Service Alliance on the west coast, it will again only be a partial settlement. Other disputes will undoubtedly crop up. In Prince Rupert we have grain handlers who are doing the same kind of job that is being done by the people in Vancouver. We have grain inspectors at both ports, all of whom are earning much less than people employed by private enterprise.

March 19, 1975
Petro-Canada

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will answer the hon. member if he will go to his own seat. I have no hesitation to enter a debate with him. I did not see any members across the aisle indicate a desire to enter the debate. Obviously, they are quite happy with the trend established by this government. This debate will continue for a long time and they will have an opportunity to speak. The after effects of this proposed company will be felt for an even longer time, so now is the time for them to enter the debate.
After I sit down I suppose the Speaker will gladly recognize any gentleman over there who wishes to make his views known. In the meantime, hon. gentlemen over there should listen to what people on this side of the House have to say, because they might learn something. In a few years from now the time will come when this mess will have to be cleaned up. Some day someone will have to face the situation, and I predict it will not be very long from now. Some day someone will have to solve the problem of this large corporation which will be exerting unfair pressure on the economy of our country.
A solution must be found to the problems of industrial and labour unrest in our country. The problems will be so severe in the next years that those fellows over there will have many opportunities to make their views known. The problem, of course, is not one-sided. The large corporations are exerting great pressure on the economy of our country. It is for that reason I believe parliament at the present time would be much better served if the government had brought before us, rather than the Petro-Can legislation, the combines legislation which would give us an opportunity to place some restrictions on the big combines, the large corporations which are exerting great pressure on many individuals and small businesses in our country.
Recently I became aware of one of these situations. An oil company in Canada has established a rental formula for its franchise holders. I suppose it is because of similar action that the government feels compelled to take over the activities of these companies and run them on behalf of the Canadian people. The fact is, of course, that the government's purpose is to take over private enterprise by regulation and to limit the powers that are being exerted by these pressure groups on the people of Canada. Of course, if that should happen and the government stayed out of everything else, the people of Canada would have the opportunity to limit the powers of the government. However, my fear and the fear of most of my colleagues is that by the time the government explores for petroleum resources, distributes petroleum resources and has complete control over all the energy in this country and everything else, the people of Canada will have lost control over the government and an election will be meaningless.
Every day there are indications of graft, price fixing and many kinds of charges. This is a serious situation. It is a direct result of government being involved in business and meddling in private enterprise. If this situation continues, the people of our country will lose control. The people to my left in the New Democratic Party always have been very outspoken about some of these large corporations. It should be interesting to them to know that there are in our party people who have also expressed reservations about
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Penner).]
some of the freedoms and actions these corporations have enjoyed.
Perhaps I might go back to the case involving the oil company which I mentioned earlier. It brought out a rental formula under which it will be charging rent to the service station operators throughout the country on the basis of 16 per cent of the gross profit. The gross profit is the margin between the cost of the sale and the purchase price of the merchandise. When it comes to the sale of labour, there is a gross margin and the oil company considers all labour at gross margin. I have taken up this matter with the oil company and have said it is no better than the federal government which charges a tax on the royalties they pay to the provinces. This, in fact, is the case because the company is charging its own franchise holders a tax and rent on money they do not even earn because it is paid out to people they hire.
I am attempting to illustrate that it is this government's responsibility to regulate the conduct of large corporations and large and small businesses. If the government did this, it would receive the support of the opposition party when it brings in its combines legislation containing regulatory measures to control the conduct of people who exert undue pressure on Canadians. I refer not only to the large businesses and corporations but also to the unions and other groups within our society.
Surely, however, it is not the role of the government to completely regulate and control private enterprise in these business matters, because governments are not geared to manage businesses. As I look around this House, I see that most of my colleagues are lawyers and some are doctors. I have dealt with professional people in private life, and whenever I have run into a poor businessman he has been a lawyer or a doctor. With all respect to my colleagues, I might say that when I become involved in difficulty in business I might hire a lawyer to bail me out, but I surely would not have him run my business. In fact, I even ask my accountants-who tell me all the mistakes I have made-if they are so smart, why are they not rich?
It is a fact that these people have grown up through the professions, but with all respect to them I say that when elected to parliament, if they would concentrate on the purpose for which government is set up this institution would be a better place. If the government enters business, these professional people do not have a clue. This is well demonstrated if we analyse the financial statements of Air Canada, the CNR, CMHC, the Post Office and the CBC. I could mention 120 more. They do not have a clue, and if it were not for that barrel without a bottom they would all be bankrupt.
As we do away with incentives, with responsible conduct and with the work ethic, as we shy away from the responsibility of balancing books at the end of the month, Canadian taxpayers will suffer. There will be the day when in front of a wicket on which it says "Pay" there will be no line-up, and in front of the wicket on which it says "Hand-outs" there will be a long line-up-except for the fact that the barrel will run dry some day. Signs of the difficulties which this government will be experiencing in carrying out its social contract are already evident

throughout the country in the tightening up of unemployment insurance benefits and the reduction in hand-outs, because as we confiscate and take over private business we will be denying ourselves the benefits of the revenue from the taxes that businesses have traditionally paid.
I am disappointed and concerned about the fact that members of only one party in the House today have expressed their views on some of these matters. The incorporation of Petro-Can is an attack on the foundation of our system. It is a departure from everything on which this country has been built, and it is disappointing to me that so few people have expressed this fact today and shown their concern. What we are doing today will be with us for a long time to come; the effects will be felt for a long time, because once the damage is done it is very hard-in most cases impossible-to undo it.
Petro-Can will not be able to exploit our energy reserves without the help of private enterprise. It will not be able to distribute energy as efficiently as private enterprise, and it will most certainly not be able to market the products as well as private enterprise. Of course, Canadians will suffer because the climate that will be created with the incorporation of this company will motivate private enterprise to look to other areas of the world in which to carry on their activities. The loss will be felt by Canadian taxpayers in particular.
