speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I am very pleased to take up the challenge of the previous speaker and to offer a few comments in support of this bill. I feel very strongly about it and I want to start out by saying that I congratulate the minister. This parliament is fortunate to have a minister of his capabilities and courage. This is probably one of the most difficult portfolios because of the changing world scene, and I think it is one that has been handled most capably by the minister for the past two years.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
I want to personally endorse the establishment of Petro-Can. The minister knows I support it strongly. Shortly after the Christmas recess I held a number of town hall meetings in my riding and my constituents from Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe told me that the next time I come back to town hall meetings I should bring them the bill that establishes Petro-Can. I am glad to be contributing toward that objective.
Parliament must do everything in its power to make Canada as self-sufficient as possible in both energy and food. I am pleased that we are acting on the Farm Credit Act, on the agricultural stabilization bill and on other farm legislation in the area of food production. This government has a good record in the area of energy, as is evidenced in the establishment of a one-price oil system across Canada, the establishment of the export tax, the re-evaluation of our capability to export gas and oil, the acceleration of natural gas exploration and the way in which the Mackenzie Valley pipeline question is being handled.
Also, I am a very strong supporter of the Syncrude involvement, of Panarctic, and so on, particularly in the area of electrical energy through CANDU technology. But
Petro-Canada
what we really need to do is add substantially to the entire energy picture in Canada at present through the establishment of Petro-Can or a government agency which could enter into a joint venture with industry and involve itself in the technology and the negotiating of energy contracts on behalf of Canadians.
To my knowledge, not many issues have come before parliament which have separated political philosophies as much as most of our energy debates, this one in particular. Members of the official opposition have been almost unanimous in saying that we should leave the energy industry entirely alone, give the companies every tax consideration and everything they ask for, and allow industry to operate virtually free of any guidelines. The NDP have argued the case for the nationalization of much of the industry. I think that the correct position is the one taken by the minister and this party, to issue strong guidelines and policies for the industry for the benefit of all Canadians, to establish a tax structure that is fair to the petroleum industry as well as to other industries that are taxed, and which is also fair to all Canadians and, now, with the help of Petro-Can, to enter into joint ventures with the petroleum industry.
I was interested to hear the speech of the critic of the official opposition. It is an interesting fact that since his speech he has not been in the House to hear the rest of the debate. That shows how interested he really is in this entire matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: That is not true.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
The point of view expressed by him was that there was really no need for government involvement, and that the petroleum industry should be left free to operate in the way it wants; that energy should be left entirely to private enterprise. Surely his party must be aware of the majority of public opinion in this regard. Most people to whom we have talked say they want very close control over the development of our resources in the future and over our petroleum industry.
Back in June of last year I attended a meeting of the Committee for an Independent Canada at which a resolution was passed by a majority vote to nationalize one of the major multinational petroleum companies. This is an organization made up of people from all political parties, people who are really concerned about the future of this country and who feel strongly about it. I would not have supported that resolution, but I consider it to be a strong expression of opinion of a large segment of the Canadian population. I think we can really say that when the best interests of the multinational petroleum companies have coincided with Canada's best interests, they have done a good job. However, when they have not coincided I must ask whether it has been in Canada's best interests.
The basic objective of the whole equation is an adequate, secure supply of reasonably-priced energy for all Canadians. We want to be very careful in evaluating arguments put forth by members on the opposite side who say that private enterprise can do it completely on their own and do it better. I think it would make sense to multinational petroleum companies certainly to go where the best deal is, where they can make the best profit. I ask members of the House whether they really think that

March 19, 1975
Petro-Canada
Canada should be involved in some kind of auction with other countries to see which country can give the best tax structure and the biggest incentives to oil companies, because if we enter into that situation all we will do is ensure artificially high returns to those companies and we will certainly not be acting in the best interests of the people whom we represent.
Also, if we are to accept the arguments put forward by the opposition, it could well be that in moving the Canadian price to the world price we would find that Canadians would be paying a higher price for their own resource than Americans, for the same energy. It would be paradoxical for us, as the exporter of oil to the United States, to be paying more for our domestic oil than would be the case with the people to whom we are exporting it.
The amounts we are talking about are not small, because when we were considering in committee the question of the involvement of the government in Syncrude-I think I am quoting the figures correctly-we were told that the expected world price of oil will probably be about $13.50 per barrel by 1978, around $15 by 1984, and perhaps as high as $30 by the year 2000. Therefore, if we are talking about leaving it entirely to the discretion of the industry and allowing oil to work its way up to the world price, that is the kind of impact there will be on Canadians and on the Canadian industrial base.
I was somewhat amazed by the point of view put forward earlier today by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) when he was making his critique of Crown corporations. If we followed his point of view we would have a wonderful country for those people surrounded by the golden horseshoe, where there is much prosperity. But I ask him, what about equal opportunity for all Canadians; and in expressing that point of view does he really care about those who do not have the opportunities of Canadians who live in areas of prosperity?
Canadians should be very proud of the role Crown corporations have played in the development of this country. The efficiency and profitability of a Crown corporation versus a private concern could be argued, but do not forget that the Crown corporation, essentially, is established in the majority of cases to benefit the whole of Canada and to operate in areas where it is not profitable for private companies to do so, or to do so at a rate which people in those areas can afford. I refer to the excellent job done by the CNR, Air Canada, and other Crown corporations.
If the point of view expressed earlier today had been followed in the past we would not now have the Atomic Energy Commission of Canada. In terms of the entire energy question which we are considering, I think we would have very real concern about the future if it were not for the excellent work of that commission. Outstanding people with leadership qualities have taken a strong stand on the whole question, and today under the commission's licence we have some of the best technology anywhere in the world with regard to energy. I hope this will be the role Petro-Canada will play.
I disagreed strongly with the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) who said the other evening that we
[Mr. Milne. 1
should just re-fund Panarctic and let it fool around in a small area of the far north. The purpose of Petro-Canada is to be a major factor in the petroleum industry within Canada, and in doing so to be staffed with strong leadership people who will work for the benefit of all the people we are trying to help.
I would like to say a word about the position put forward by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) in terms of our involvement in Syncrude. He said the government should have taken over total control of Syncrude and moved quickly to nationalize a large corporation such as Exxon. In reply to that, I think there is only so much money the government has at its disposal and it is a question of where to spend it in order to get the most leverage. If those two projects were undertaken on the basis put forward by the New Democratic Party, then what financial strength would we have in the future to meet the next energy situation which comes along? I think we want to participate one way or another in a large number of projects on a joint venture basis, rather than invest totally in one or two and then be unable to participate in the rest.
As I visualize Petro-Can, I take issue with much of the viewpoint put forward on the opposite side whereby Petro-Can is being painted as an organization which will muscle out the present industry; that it will be the biggest competitor, and so on. Surely the basic role of Petro-Can will be in the area of joint venture, where it is deemed in the public interest that certain developments should take place and at a certain rate. That would be where Petro-Can would be involved, and presumably on most occasions involved on a joint venture basis rather than as a basic competitor of any of the individual companies.
I think there are some pretty strong precedents set by governments not only in this country but other countries-certainly by provincial governments-for government having a strong role in this area. After all, when the United States was experiencing real difficulty under President Roosevelt, the way out of that difficulty was to establish the Tennessee Valley Authority, which I think most members of this House would agree is a very strong economic development tool.
Nearly all the provincial governments, regardless of their political faith, have moved to set up provincial commissions for hydroelectric power. They have done so because they are concerned about equal opportunity for all the people within the province and they are concerned about having power at the lowest possible cost upon which to build an industrial base.
We are talking about the tremendously escalating cost of energy in the future; we are talking about oil which may cost $30 a barrel by the year 2000. Because of this, if ever there was a time for the government to move for protection against that eventuality, to establish a strong Canadian base in the petroleum industry and to have some influence in that area, the time is certainly now.
I would think that one of the very strong points-and hon. members should realize this-for Petro-Can is in terms of holding the licence for technology. Whoever controls technology really controls the game, and if Petro-Can has enough technology under its licence it may very well be possible to join people not even associated with the
March 19, 1975

petroleum industry in some development aspects because Petro-Can can contribute the technology and the other concerns can perhaps contribute the majority of the financing.
I would think that through Petro-Can the government would want to participate where and when necessary, and by having a large amount of technology under its licence it would be possible for Petro-Can to get a great deal of leverage for a small amount of investment. I hope Petro-Can will move very quickly to assemble a group of highly qualified people. We are operating in a very difficult industry, one which requires extremely competent people, and I think it is not easy to have this expertise without being actively involved in the field. By having these people working for Petro-Can the government will have a much tighter grip on the petroleum industry and a better understanding of it.
I hope, also, that Petro-Can, along with the government, will be able to take a very broad look at the entire energy situation. I think one of the major problems here is that projects are going forward when they should, and perhaps there is the problem of too many projects going ahead at the same time. As the hon. member from Fort William has mentioned on a number of occasions, the real necessity if that these projects be staged. I think this would require, under Petro-Can, motivating some and perhaps not participating in others, so that we have a good input in terms of how the projects are coming on stream.
As the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine) said in his speech last night, there is very grave concern about the absence of research under Canadian auspices carried out by the petroleum industry. That should be a major role for Petro-Can. If research is totally foreign-controlled, I do not think we will have the leverage we should.
I want to make a few comments in taking up the challenge of hon. members opposite that government members are not speaking in support of this bill. Of all the bills we will be introducing in the initial part of this thirtieth parliament, Madam Speaker, I think this is one of the most important. I should like to ask hon. members opposite where some of their own members from Ontario and the maritimes stand on this bill. I have not seen many of them stand up and oppose Petro-Can in the way that the official lobbyists from Calgary have been doing. I should like to see members from Ontario and the maritimes stand up and be counted so that their constituents can evaluate how they feel about Petro-Can.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened to the hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne) very closely because I wanted to know why he felt the bill was an important piece of legislation. He talked about the government having control over the oil industry and over energy. Certainly, the government has demonstrated its control over the oil industry and energy without having a national oil company. The hon. member talked about Petro-Can having to put together a team of technological experts who could entice money from the private sector. He said that he hoped Petro-Can would gather such people around it, and gave a long, rambling dissertation but failed to point out any need whatsoever for the bill. That is the only conclusion I can come to after listening to him.
The history of nationalized oil companies is of great interest. The British government established British Petroleum and took 50 per cent ownership to assure an oil supply for its navy. At that time it was not thought there was any oil in Great Britain and they wanted a company of their own to explore in the Middle East and off their shores. Aquatane was formed for similar reasons by the French government, to explore off their shores. Most national oil companies that have had any success have been formed to do the exploration outside the boundaries of their country. This government, however, is setting up a national oil company to do exploration and development with, I suppose, a chain of refineries and selling mechanisms throughout Canada, eventually. I suppose the exploration is to be done mainly within Canada, although that point has not been clarified.
An interesting argument has taken place, regarding oil and energy, in this House and across the country in the last couple of years. Canada has never had a huge amount of proven reserves in relation to total world supply. Many people think that Alberta is rich in oil and that Canada should have enough oil for years and years to come. Without taking the tar sands into consideration, the known reserves of conventional oil in Canada are very small indeed in relation to total world supply and world needs. What enticed international and Canadian companies to explore in Alberta in the last number of years was the stability of this country's government and the manner in which exploration units, Canadian or otherwise, could operate due to the stability of the economic climate. They felt their investment was safer here than in the Middle East, Indonesia, Mexico, South America or some other places where there was greater known potential.
In the last four years, however, the Liberal government has pretty well destroyed that stable economic climate for the oil industry. It is no wonder that we see consternation amongst Canadian and international oil companies and the international finance which has to support these companies in exploration. They are now somewhat reluctant to invest in exploration in Canada. Why, and how, did this come about, and what are our reserves?
A great argument developed in Canada in recent years about Alberta's known reserves and whether they

Petro-Canada
belonged to Canada or to Alberta. In my opinion that question was needless: the reserves belong to Canada. The Fathers of Confederation stated quite clearly that our natural resources can best be looked after by the government closest to the resource. By "looked after" I mean that the government closest to the resource can best gauge the time for development and the quantity to be developed. For the services that the developing government must provide, it could and should be expected to take a royalty.
That was really what the Fathers of Confederation said, and I think it is the way most Canadians feel today. The resources belong to Canada and they are to be developed and managed by the government closest to the resource, whether it be coal in Cape Breton, coal in British Columbia or uranium in Ontario. It is a resource to be developed, the time for its development and the quantity to be developed is to be determined by the government closest to it, and a royalty charge for the facilities necessary for development is to be charged as an expense to the resource development company.
In his budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) changed all that and stated that the royalty charged by the province will no longer be allowed as an expense to the resource development company. That destroyed a little bit of the economic climate that used to exist in Canada. Prior to that the OPEC nations, acting as a cartel, forced up the world price of oil. What did the federal government do? It must have known that oil exploration is a costly business, that oil which is easiest to find is found first and that which is harder to develop comes on stream at a later stage of the process. It is logical to assume that oil is still to be found in this country but that its development will be a costly process. Responding to the move of the OPEC nations, the government put a ceiling on oil prices in this country. Prices went from $1.19 per barrel to $4, and then to $6.50. After the next first ministers' meeting which is to be on April 1, oil prices may or may not go up again.
If the minister had the best interests of Canada at heart, he ought to have said that in order to encourage stability in the oil industry Canadian oil sold domestically would sell for less than the international price, but that its price would be the equivalent of 50 per cent, 75 per cent, or what you will, of the international price. At least the oil industry in Canada should have known what to expect. Prices could have adjusted automatically. As it is, Canadian and foreign-owned oil companies are at the mercy of the government. Our vital resources should not be administered in such an erratic manner.
Perhaps the government could afford to pursue its present course if our oil supplies were ample; but they are not ample. We are not possessed of ample crude oil reserves-let me put it that way. We have destroyed the confidence of the industry and harmed our chances for being self-sufficient in oil. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) said, according to an article in the Toronto Star of February 20, that we shall need to spend $100 billion to make Canada self-sufficient in oil by the year 2000. Yet he has done his best to chase exploration money from this country as quickly as possible. I am not talking about multinational oil companies; I am talking about Canadian oil companies which have

taken their money out of this country: they are looking for oil and gas in the United States and in the North Sea.
The actions of the government, particularly of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, have encouraged Canadian money to leave this country; and one of those ministers had the gall to say that we shall need to spend $100 billion on energy if this country is to be self-sufficient in energy by the year 2000. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources made several mistakes. In April, 1970, he disallowed royalties in connection with exploration north of the sixtieth parallel. All kinds of oil companies which have staked out leases in our northland do not know how much royalty the federal government will want if and when oil for which they are exploring comes on stream. Government policy deliberately forced many companies to abandon exploration holes they had drilled north of the sixtieth parallel. What is the result? By 1977 this country will not produce enough gas to supply Ontario, Montreal and parts of the United States. By 1978 we shall begin cutting down on oil exports as we shall not have enough oil to meet our own requirements. The National Energy Board said that by 1982 we shall become a net importer of oil.
There is no need for Canada to be in this position. The government is responsible. Our largest known reserves of oil are in the tar sands. What did the government and the minister do that was wrong in connection with the tar sands?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: Nothing.

speechtext: I am glad to note someone is listening.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: Glad and surprised.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Let me list four ways in which the government was wrong. First, it said that the price of tar sands oil would be frozen or controlled. You cannot treat tar sands oil in the way you treat conventional oil. It is not the same; it needs costly machinery for extraction and the extraction process is work-intensive. Common sense should tell you that when you embark on a project which will take many man-hours to complete and which requires large quantities of expensive machinery, the end price, given the inflationary conditions of the past two years, will go up. That is exactly what happens. This holds true if you are developing a conventional oil well or tar sands oil. The government decided to freeze the price of conventional oil. That was a political decision. It should have said that tar sands oil will be sold at the world price. It did not say this even though it knew that we were living in inflationary times and that the project would need a great deal of expensive machinery. This omission was its first mistake.
Its second mistake was this: it did not say that the Syncrude ground rules would apply to every company seeking to develop the tar sands. The government had to include the Great Canadian Oil Sands company in the Syncrude-type guidelines; the company was already in operation and the government had no choice. The government made special royalty provisions for Syncrude, provisions which it did not extend to other parties which might seek to develop the tar sands.

The National Energy Board said that a new tar sands project should come on stream every two years. Home Oil, a Canadian oil company a majority shareholder of which is Consumers' Gas of Toronto, asked the government for concessions similar to those given to Syncrude. The government refused but said it would work out a deal with the company. You cannot expect companies to compete with one another but not work under the same ground rules. The government's mistake was in not laying down rules which would apply to every company seeking to develop the tar sands. The same rules should apply to royalties and tax limits. Rules applying in the same way to all the companies would greatly have enhanced the prospects for the future development of the tar sands.
The next mistake which was made in connection with the tar sands project applied particularly to Syncrude. The government should have said, "We shall allow a company which comes in to develop an oil extraction plant in the tar sands to export a percentage of that oil." Why? It was because we needed foreign money for the development of these tar sands in our own interest. The minister might have said to Atlantic Richfield, "For every two barrels you get out of the tar sands you will be able to export one." In those circumstances perhaps Atlantic Richfield might have been able to raise the necessary capital in the United States and elsewhere. Instead, the minister closed off export opportunities.
The Japanese for some time have been interested in the Canadian tar sands but we have effectively discouraged them from coming in and taking part in this venture. The Japanese are dependent on imports to meet all their energy needs; they take about 17 per cent of total OPEC exports so they are obviously very interested in access to a source of energy. The Japanese would gladly invest in the tar sands project provided some formula were reached which warranted the use of their money to benefit Canada and Canadians as well as their own particular interest. The government has only itself to blame when it finds Canada likely to run short of oil in the relatively near future.
One only has to look at any geological study of the region to see where the best potential for future oil discoveries lies. A while ago I mentioned the regulations which were discontinued on April 10 concerning future exploration north of the 60th parallel. Mr. Speaker, that area is very important because it is still solely under the jurisdiction of the federal government. Most geologists agree, on the basis of seismic studies, that the delta area of the Mackenzie River and the Beaufort Sea, where you find the tertiary land formation, are the areas in which most of the possibilities lie. I might point out that something like 70 per cent of the world supply is found in this type of land formation. The Venezuelan oil fields and the recent find in Mexico come to mind in this connection. The only Canadian region in which such a formation occurs is in the Arctic.
The Prudhoe Bay find most likely extends right out into the Beaufort Sea and includes the Mackenzie River delta. Yet we have discouraged exploration there. It is true that some companies are still exploring in the territory, but they are doing so only in order to hold on to their leases.
Petro-Canada
Will Petro-Canada or another government-controlled company be able to do any better than Panarctic which is already operating in the Arctic? That is the question which the hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe should really try to answer when he talks to his constituents, the Liberals he meets in the town halls.
As I say, our best potential is in the high Arctic, the delta of the Mackenzie River, and the Beaufort Sea. Panarctic is already up there and it is 45 per cent owned by the government of Canada. This 45 per cent gives the federal government control over the entire operation of Panarctic as well as the power to veto any proposed operation, or any change of the mix of shareholders. Thus, Canada's best potential lies in an area over which the federal government already has control, and in which a government controlled consortium is already operating. I fail to see why another petroleum corporation should be needed in these circumstances.
I do not believe any major oil company has the slightest fear of competing with a government owned oil company. I would certainly regard a private company as being poor operators if they feared competition from a government corporation. It is not fear of competition which arises here; it is fear of an unfair ball game. In the last four years, particularly in the last two years, we have seen continual changes in the regulations governing exploration for oil in Canada.
The government is now attempting to argue that the creation of a public petroleum corporation will instill greater confidence into the oil industry. It will do nothing of the kind. We shall not be able to entice oil companies to resume exploration in Canada on the previous scale, or induce them to increase the pace of exploration if we set up a Canadian exploration company to engage in operations of its own in this field. The atmosphere the government created, an atmosphere of distrust, will further encourage the companies to stay in the North Sea, or the United States, or somewhere else.
I note that the bill makes provision for a capital structure of around $500 million, which is a mere drop in the bucket when measured against the $100 billion the minister said it would cost to ensure that Canada is self-sufficient in energy supplies between now and the year 2,000. Rather than create uncertainty and concentration among the exploration companies we should now be moving to create a better economic climate to encourage exploration in Canada.
We are more knowledgeable than we were at the time the world oil crisis first started and the OPEC nations realized they had a monopoly and could set prices. The experts said that the OPEC nations would lower their price for oil to about half of what the price increased to eventually. The price quickly shot up to $12 or $14 a barrel, but the experts said that by the fall of 1974 the OPEC nations would back off and would sell oil at somewhere in the neighbourhood of $6 a barrel.
The OPEC nations held meeting after meeting, and then told the world that one of their key problems was their desire to protect their endowment over the long run against inflation and currency devaluation. They have

March 19, 1975
Petro-Canada
said that they will hold the present world price of oil if the oil importing nations will give them some assurance that their currencies will not be further devalued. So we must realize that the OPEC nations have no intention of lowering the world price of oil, and we should adjust our economy accordingly.
Is this bill to set up Petro-Canada and to give it authority to enter the hydrocarbons industry really necessary? Under Polysar the petrochemical industry has been expanded, so this bill is not required from that aspect. There is no question that Canada will be in need of money to supply Canadians with their energy requirements. Right now in the Arctic, feasibility and environmental studies are taking place before the Berger commission which is inquiring into the possibility of building a Mackenzie valley gas pipe line. So far as the all Canadian route is concerned, commonly known as the maple leaf route, the Foothills Gas Company estimates the project will cost Canadians $4 billion.

speechtext:
I hear hon. members saying terrible and shame, but I do not think they are taking this debate very seriously. It is their government that has contributed to this increased cost by allowing inflation to run rampant.
Is this the best way of spending $500 million to ensure that Canadians will have ample energy supplies in the years ahead? I do not think it is. I think it will create greater fears in regard to oil exploration. It will cause more private capital to leave Canada and not return, because investors will be afraid of the ground rules the government is laying down.
From time to time we see greater demand for revenues from the oil and gas industry. Off the east coast near Sable Island there is estimated to be about one trillion cubic feet of gas. The oil companies are not interested in extracting this gas because the small quantity, and the oil royalties demanded by the provinces make it uneconomic. Further possibilities of exploration for gas lie in the north off Labrador, and these are very good indeed. But here again the government has been negligent in working out agreements with the province of Newfoundland as to which government has authority off the coast of Labrador.
There is much the government can do to create a better climate for energy exploration, and this would go a long way toward bringing more money back from the private sector to the energy exploration area. This bill will only discourage such capital flow.
It is estimated that in the Mackenzie River delta there are eight to 12 trillion cubic feet of gas reserves at the present time. It is estimated that Panarctic has found about 12 trillion cubic feet of gas in what is commonly called the high Arctic. It is believed that if a gas pipe line could be built down the Mackenzie valley, then further exploration would take place and greater reserves would be revealed. In fact optimistic estimates of the possible reserves in the high Arctic are in the neighbourhood of 150 trillion cubic feet.

With all this gas, Madam Speaker, one wonders whether we will be deficient in the supply of gas by 1977 or 1978. But we have witnessed the short-sighted policies of this government, and this Petro-Can bill is just one more. It may satisfy the political aspirations of some of the minister's backbenchers, but it will not satisfy the need of all Canadians across Canada for sufficient supplies of energy to heat their homes, their factories, and to supply the furnaces in steel and other industries.
It is often said that there is a lot of natural gas in Alberta. We are using our natural gas at the rate of roughly 2.3 trillion cubic feet a year. Alberta has reserves in the neighbourhood of 70 trillion cubic feet, though these have yet to reach the marketable state. Some socialists believe that the known gas reserves in what might be called the Suffield area of southeastern Alberta will bail us out of any short term difficulties in which we find ourselves. There are about three trillion cubic feet of gas reserves in the Suffield area, less than one year's supply. So if anyone thinks that rapid drilling for this gas will immediately alleviate the shortfall that we see ahead of us in 1977 and 1978, they are just kidding themselves and nobody else.
In addition there is in this area what is commonly referred to as the British block. There is an experimental research area there of huge dimensions where, from time to time, the army explodes some dynamite, blows a hole in the ground, and determines how much dynamite is needed to penetrate the earth to a certain distance-it is about that simple. They test-fire a few rockets in that area as well, along with small arms artillery. I point this out because this testing takes place under contract with the British government. There are no publicly known negotiations taking place to end this sort of exploration in that area. You cannot go out and explore for natural gas with that kind of experimental testing of firearms, dynamite, and the like going on. Everyone knows the fire potential of a gas and oil exploration area.
Somewhere down the line we have to make a decision in respect of this $100 billion energy bill and how best it should be met so that we are not left with a deficiency of energy. Part of that money should go toward encouraging further development of our most potential areas such as the Mackenzie River delta and the Beaufort Sea. The fastest and easiest way to encourage more development there is to move forward in an orderly manner with the development of the Mackenzie River delta area.

The purpose of Bill C-8, if passed, is to establish a Crown owned corporation with the authority to engage in all phases of an integrated energy company operating in Canada as well as in foreign countries. The corporation can engage in all normal energy-related company activities in addition to activities which it may deem expedient for, or conducive to, the furtherance of the objects of the corporation.
Although not specifically stated in the proposed bill, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) will run the corporation. The chairman of the board, the president and directors, and replacements as they become necessary, will be appointed by the Governor in Council, and evidently the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Thus it is clear that the minister will run the whole show.
The corporation will receive initial authorized capital totalling $500 million in return for 100 common shares. The initial subscription will come from the consolidated revenue fund administered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), in other words, right from the pockets of the taxpayers. The shares of the corporation are not transferable, so no one will be allowed to buy any stock in this company. The shares are to be held by the Minister of Finance in trust for the government; thus the government is the sole owner.
As mentioned, the powers of the corporation are extremely wide and provide for a great variety of endeavours not necessarily dealing with hydrocarbons or

energy. The corporation may obtain additional money from the Crown, or it can borrow and issue debentures on the open market, guaranteed, or not, by the Crown. For the purpose of the act the corporation will be an agent of the government, and consequently any property acquired by it will be the property of the government. The corporation will be bound by all laws and natural resource conservation regulations of any province in which it operates.
The corporation may purchase the federal government interest in the PanArctic Company, under certain conditions, and all dividends payable will be paid to the Crown. However, there is no mention in the bill that the corporation is to be run as a profitable venture. There are certain provisions in the Canada Corporations Act which this corporation does not need to obey, such as those in respect of selection of directors, bylaws, books of the company, notices, etc. May I call it six o'clock, Madam Speaker.

speechtext:
On February 26, my colleague the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Stewart) put a question to the Minister of Justice in his capacity as minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. The question, at page 3600
of Hansard, reads:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice in his capacity as Minister of Justice in his capacity as minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. In view of the fact that there are approximately 14,000 boxcars locked in the prairies because of the current public service strike and, because there are about 28 ships now waiting in Vancouver harbour with escalating demurrage charges being calculated on a daily basis, would the minister indicate to the House whether he has formulated any contingency plan for the movement of this export grain in an effort to ensure that Canada's international reputation as a grain supplier is not subject to further humiliation?
Listen to the comforting answer of the minister:
Mr. Speaker, a number of plans are being looked at, both in connection with the immediate period and also in connection with an attempt to catch up as quickly as possible when conditions return to normal.
It would seem to be appropriate tonight, Mr. Speaker, now that the Minister of Justice is in a more ebullient mood, for him to come before the House and tell us what plans he had in mind on February 26 when there were 28 ships in Vancouver harbour and 14,000 boxcars locked in the prairies. Perhaps the minister can tell us how many ships are in Vancouver harbour now. If he cannot, then there are a number of citizens in the city I come from who could inform him that there are approximately 40 ships
4272

March 19, 1975

waiting there. If there were 14,000 boxcars locked in the prairies on February 26, there are certainly more now.
It seems to me it is incumbent upon the government to tell us exactly what is going to be done to get this grain moving and to assure the House that in the future we are not going to have a repetition of the staggering number of days lost by work stoppages that have plagued this particular harbour to date. I should like to bring to the attention of the House a telegram sent to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) today by the president of the Vancouver Grain Exporters Association, which reads:
Your office is quoted today worldwide for having stated yesterday "public interest has not yet been hurt enough to warrant government intervention". Having at heart the whole Canadian grain trade both east and west from Ottawa, we find such statement, if correctly quoted, bordering aberrance. During the crop year started August 1, 1974, grain exports ex Vancouver have been stopped by strikes during 68 work days out of 165, based on five day week less holidays, or during 41.2 per cent of straight time.
Those are facts, Mr. Speaker, and they have led to a situation where the Minister of Justice in charge of the Wheat Board is going to have to tell the House what the contingency plans are that he talked about on February 26. I want to say to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that it is not enough for him to take the view that because we have heard tonight that accord has been reached, problems have ended in Vancouver. The telegram to the Prime Minister from the Vancouver Grain Exporters Association continues:
Your letter of March 4 in answer to ours of February 20 arrived here on March 13.
I am sorry the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) is not in the House tonight so that we might get some answers as to when that particular problem is going to be solved. The telegram continues:
Yours is a standard type answer given over and over as years go by on each strike situation. It sadly proves a lack of leadership between contracts or from strike to strike to avoid such costly occurrences.
It is legitimate to ask tonight whether the government has any contingency plans to move the grain that has piled up, and also whether the government has any idea what it is going to do to break the pattern of strikes that have stopped grain shipments on the west coast. Let us look at the statistics. We have now reached a situation where there are over 40 vessels waiting to load grain; between August 1, 1974, and today approximately 70 shipping days have been lost; Canada is 900,000 tons behind on grain shipments due to China in 1974; China is presently negotiating to buy one million tons of grain from Canada in 1975 and a portion of this is in jeopardy because of Canada's poor delivery service. That jeopardy is not going to be relieved just because, by a lot of hard work on the part of some people, the present PSAC strike seems to have been settled. Our customers are going to look at the record and say-they cannot say anything else, on the basis of experience-that Canada is not a reliable supplier.
The Minister of Justice said an extraordinary thing yesterday. He said in the House that although the Japanese are now buying grain in the United States and Australia because they could not get supplies from Vancouver, United States ports have not been without strikes. Mr. Speaker, I might remind the minister that since 1972 there has not been a strike on the west coast of the United

States that has stopped grain shipments. I think the minister must concede that their record has been considerably better than ours, and at the present time they are entering into negotiations which will last until 1978. In trying to evade the facts, and to some degree, I suggest, his responsibility by saying that other countries have strikes, the minister ought to be careful what country he is talking about. No shipments of grain have been stopped on the west coast of the United States since 1972.
I was talking to a Canadian grain exporter who had arrived back here a day or so ago from Tokyo. He said that he had never experienced a worse attitude among the grain importers, many of whom are threatening not even to bother tendering for new orders. Our record is so appalling that customers have no confidence in our future ability to deliver. It is incumbent on the government to tell the House and country what it intends to do. On March 26 the Minister of Justice told the House of his contingency plans. He said, as recorded at page 3600 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, a number of plans are being looked at-
I suppose one of them will not be needed because of what has happened this evening. I continue quoting:
-both in connection with the immediate period and also in connection with an attempt to catch up as quickly as possible when conditions return to normal.
The minister should tell the House the extent of those plans and of what they consist. The House should not assume that because difficulties between the PSAC and Treasury Board have been partially resolved there are not serious problems at the port of Vancouver. The world's largest grain carrier is tied up waiting for a shipment of grain for Bangladesh. I assume all members know how badly that grain is needed in Bangladesh. That ship can carry 30,000 tons but only 10,000 tons have been loaded. The remainder of the cargo is tied up in boxcars and elevators. The ship has been docked for months. I was glad to hear that finally something is to be done. A Vancouver churchman said to me, "In the name of Christian decency, let us do something to get this ship loaded and on its way."
Members representing western constituencies say day after day that there are serious difficulties on the west coast and on the prairies and that our reputation in the world of commerce is suffering. Therefore, we have not been overstating the case. If any members doubt my word, let them telephone Vancouver and talk to people who have watched the harbour filling with ships and have been laid off because of this strike. The government should also tell us what it is doing with regard to its so-called consensus. What will it do in future? What is it doing in its search for consensus across this land?

speechtext:
I see the Minister of Justice is talking to some hon. members opposite. I do not know if he is trying to enlighten them or persuading them to make more noise. It is high time the government told this House about the consensus we hear so much about, as these strikes are taking place because of lack of consensus. Rising inflation rates have made increasing numbers of people at the lower end of the wage scale frightened, desperate and militant. They are prepared to strike because, basically they feel their security is threatened. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) have talked about consensus, but nowhere has the government indicated in which direction it wants to go and what its objectives are. So long as the government talks but does nothing to encourage restraint, consensus will not be achieved. I am afraid the Minister of Justice will need to talk about something else.
Basically, the government has asked the working people of this country to stick their necks out and, because inflation is rampant, to give up some of their bargaining power. But the government has abdicated its responsibilities. By not laying down adequate policies, the government has eroded confidence in the country. The Minister of Labour has talked about establishing a Canada labour council. I understand that the cabinet has discussed this proposal, but the government has not said what it will do about it. Surely this House is entitled to know the steps being taken to form the proposed Canada labour council. We ought to know who will be represented on it and what the objectives of the council are to be.
In summary let me say this. The government for weeks has refused to face its responsibilities and to consider that basically what we are dealing with affects the national interest. The government has not responded to the emergency. I remind hon. members that since 1972 the government has intervened four times in grain disputes and ordered, through legislative measures, grain shipments to be resumed. On August 31, 1972, the then minister of labour said, as recorded at page 3901 of Hansard for that date:
-there are occasions when parliament must deal with situations, when the full resort to economic warfare by strike or lockout so impairs the ability of others to carry on their activities that it can be said to be against the national interest for the work stoppage to continue. Parliament in this case was recalled as a last resort when it was evident that the ports on the west coast would not resume operations for some weeks if normal collective bargaining procedures were allowed to take their course.
He went on to say, as recorded at page 3902:
By far and away the hardest hit at this time is the grain economy on its external markets. This important sector of the economy is presently in the greatest jeopardy should the ports remain closed. British Columbia, too, has an export-oriented economy-
If it was in the national interest in 1972, just before the election, to pass special legislation for keeping the grain moving, why has it not been in the national interest in the last several weeks to take action which will keep grain moving? I ask all hon. members present, many of whom were also in the House in August, 1973, to remember the arguments put forward by the present Minister of Labour. He said at that time that conditions in the country were affecting the national interest and that we had to pass legislation. In 1974, during the election campaign, relevant sections of the Canada Labour Code had to be invoked to
Grain Shipments
make sure that the grain handlers did not go on strike. That action was in the national interest. In October, 1974, parliament legislated the grain handlers back to work. It was said that that action was in the national interest as we could not afford to see grain movement stopped. In the present instance the government has for weeks refused to act even though the scales, to use the Prime Minister's phrase, had definitely tilted against the national interest. Apparently government supporters, including the Minister of Justice, suffered a lapse of memory.

That being the case I have no intention of speaking at any length. We in this party are, of course, happy the strike has been settled. However, I do not agree a great deal of credit is deserved by the minister or the government. The strike need not have taken place. It would not have taken place if the minister and the government had been as generous to those who have been on strike for the last couple of weeks as they had been to senior government employees over the past couple of years. I shall not illustrate this contention in detail now, but we shall find occasions to demonstrate clearly the vast difference between the attitude of the government toward senior public servants and its attitude toward tens of thousands of employees in the public service who are still working for very moderate wages. However, this is not the time to do so. The strike has been settled.
We are living in difficult times. We can be certain there will be other strikes in both the public and private sectors in the next few months. This does not surprise me. We have lived through three or four years of a booming economy during which time, encouraged by the government, corporations in Canada have made increasingly large profits. They never had it so good. This being the case it is not surprising that working people, in the light of those exorbitant profits and in the light of sharp increases in the cost of living, should demand their share of increased prosperity. The government asked for this kind of situation and now we have to live with it.
I know there will be opportunities in the coming weeks to discuss what lies ahead for the country, to consider the parlous state of labour-management relations, and we in this party intend to make proposals for what the government should do, and to point out what the government has failed to do to minimize differences and avoid possible strikes and work stoppages.
We hope the government has learned some lessons from the situation we have met tonight to consider and which it helped to create. We hope that in future it will move more expeditiously, more flexibly, and with greater humanity than I believe it showed in this dispute, so that we shall

Mr. Speaker, since a settlement has been reached on the strike which motivated an urgent and special debate, according to the provisions of Standing Order 26, I say our debate has come too late.
As it frequently happens with this political system, owing to our cumbersome democratic paraphernalia, debates take place in the House after the blows have been dealt.
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised to see that Progressive Conservative members want to proceed with the debate on a problem which has already been settled. That may be a way for them to avoid tackling current issues which are still wanting a solution, especially agricultural problems in eastern Canada, which they do not understand. Anyway, Mr. Speaker, the problem we are considering has been settled. Our debate deals with the problem of feed grain supplies, the problem of the grain handlers strike which jeopardized agriculture in eastern Canada, since the supplies of Quebec were in danger of being cut off. In most cases, there were only 5 to 10 days' supplies left in several cooperative mills.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to say a few words in this debate tonight. It is indeed gratifying to all members of the House to learn the strike has been settled this afternoon, but it should be made abundantly clear that the motion that the opposition moved today was probably the log that broke the logjam as far as the strike was concerned, and forced the government to take action. So while we are debating some aspects of the grain situation it must be pointed out that in this respect the debate has been very successful, especially for the people involved in western Canada.
I should like to say a few words about the effect such a strike as this has had, and will have on farmers and on the agricultural industry in general in Canada, but first let me say that strikes of this kind of duration that have taken place, and possibly will be taking place in the future, are utter madness. The people of this country in all walks of life are becoming increasingly frustrated and dissatisfied at government inaction and at the over-all malaise that is apparent, which creates the atmosphere we have had in the past month so far as grain handling is concerned.
With regard to the effects the strike has had on the grain industry, on farmers and on the port of Vancouver, at the present time we are paying demurrage on 33 grain ships in the port. Six more grain vessels are due this week.
March 19, 1975

I understand that we will not know until the end of this week whether the longshoremen have ratified their agreement and returned to work. Some six or seven ships have left Vancouver because they could not get grain and were not prepared to wait around for a lengthy period of time.
The total amount of demurrage charges that the Canadian Wheat Board will have to pay, and consequently the farmers will have to pay, has been put at upwards of $4,000 per hour over the past number of weeks, that these grain vessels have been waiting in Vancouver harbour. This is money that will come directly out of the pockets of the farmers.
At the present time in western Canada roughly 22,000 boxcars are idle, which means approximately 50 million bushels of western grain are sitting completely tied up on the tracks. I contend that our transportation systems will be utter chaos until well on into the summer. Grain will be hauled in a criss-cross manner over the prairies, which means a great deal of inefficiency. For example, Alberta grain will have to be allocated to Thunder Bay so as to keep the stocks at Thunder Bay in proper position. Over the past three or four weeks almost all available rolling stock for grain has been filled to capacity, and one can well imagine the kind of chaos in which our whole grain transportation system will be.
According to figures provided by a very reliable source we have lost two months' movement of grain, or 50 million bushels. The minister responsible for the Wheat Board said that this grain has not really been lost, but if one talks to people in the grain trade, in effect this 50 million bushels has been lost. Grain sales are not being made at the present time, and none are being made into the future. Any sale that will be made will have to be deferred well into the next crop year.
This shows the magnitude of the problem we are discussing. Grain buyers are turning to the United States, Australia and Europe for supplies, and since the reputation of the port of Vancouver has been jeopardized I predict this kind of situation will continue. Canada's reputation as a reliable grain supplier has never been lower than at the present time, and this goes well back to the period when we were just starting to move grain in any kind of volume. Numerous contracts over the past three or four years have been switched from Canada to the United States, one being a contract for wheat with The Philippines, and another with Africa. The sad part is that both these contracts were with first time customers of Canada. One can imagine the problem we will have in regaining the confidence of these two customers specifically, and certainly there will be other cases. One of our major losses will be sales to Japan. Japan buys grain on a weekly tender basis. It has not been able to secure supplies from Canada, so consequently it will be buying from other countries.
Our farmers will be faced with these tremendous demurrage charges that have to be paid. Last year it was said we paid $17 million, and I predict that this will be about half the demurrage charges that we will be paying this coming year, taking into consideration all of the labour problems that we will be facing. Aside from that, in the past months we have seen world grain prices drop significantly. Farmers in western Canada who want to
Grain Shipments
deliver grain have been completely isolated from the markets, and they have not been able to deliver it.
Another matter of great concern, certainly to the Canadian Wheat Board and other exporters, is the fact that there was a lot of grain for movement in what is considered the high price range, $5 per bushel. This grain has not been moved, and there is a chance that some of these contracts will have to be renegotiated. One of the reasons this debate is continuing tonight can be found in the fact that Canada has the second worst reputation in labour problems of any country in the world, right next to Italy. That is why we on this side of the House felt very strongly that the government had to act by settling the strike or bringing in emergency legislation.
Perhaps these areas that service such commodities as grain and others, which affect not only regional economies but the economy of Canada as a whole, should be considered with the idea of designating them as essential services. We must certainly come to realize that some of these services are essential, and situations such as the one we have seen take place on the west coast cannot be allowed to continue.
Up until the time the motion was moved today the government had done absolutely nothing. Yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that this really was not of national importance. Let me say, in conclusion, that while in some respects it is gratifying to know that a part of the strike is over, and I remind hon. members that we are not sure that the longshoremen will go back, it is incumbent on members from those parts of the country that are affected to point out the disastrous situation which occurs when we experience prolonged strikes. It will be very interesting tonight to hear an NDP member from the prairies speak on this motion in favour of the farmers, while at the same time agreeing that grain must be moved in this country.

Madam Speaker, I should like to make a brief intervention in this debate to comment on a few of the matters that have been raised. I listened with interest to the previous speaker and his suggestion that we were serving a particular political interest in dealing with the labour situation before us, settlement of the dispute and return to work. He did not make clear the particular interest he thought we were serving, but it should have been plain to him that we are serving the system of settlement of disputes and the collective bargaining process as it exists in this country.
I want to assure you, Madam Speaker, that this government was completely aware of the consequences and significance of the work stoppage. After the presentation of the problem as viewed from the position of prairie persons interested in grain there could have been no doubt on the part of the government about the seriousness of the matter in terms of the delay and the problems associated with it. This leads to the question of how this matter ended as it did and why the government took the position it did.
I should like to refer to the statement of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) that we were involved in two strikes here rather than one, and they were overlaid one on top of the other. I should point out that during the course of negotiations in the longshoreman's strike there seemed to be a significant chance of settlement by bargaining, and even when the strike took place it looked as though settlement might be achieved at an early date through mediation. This turned out to be the case, through the skilful mediation of Mr. Kelly, Assistant Deputy Minister of Labour: a settlement was reached and will likely be ratified within the next couple of days.
The other strike that overlaid the situation and closed the whole of the port on the west coast, not just in regard to grain, meant that there was another situation in existence while the strike in the public service was continuing. It was a complicated question then as to how quickly we should intervene in a situation where the longshoremen and the management had attained a significant degree of understanding about the problem of work stoppage and particularly about the problem of grain.
As we started this debate tonight I mentioned the ratification of the settlement by the longshoremen. I hope it will be ratified and I have some confidence that it may be, because in other situations they have shown concern and understanding about the problems that the stoppage of grain inflicts upon this major industry in our country. That consciousness of the problems caused by strikes by those involved in them is an important development and growth that we need in this country. I do not think it is particularly helpful, instead of directing attention to the problems that strikes produce for society, for interested third persons to indulge in rhetoric about the need for settling strikes or the need for doing something else in the situation. That is evading the fundamental issue that exists in the labour field itself and the question of how to solve disputes.
Grain Shipments
An hon. member tonight said that strikes are madness. I have said that strikes, in their effect on innocent third parties, are barbaric. Sometimes their effects on innocent third persons are drastic. But I have also said that we should consider the history of the strike and why working men have so readily used it. They have resorted to the strike weapon when there is not some other fair way to resolve a dispute.
Many of this country have said that an alternative to the strike should be found, that some form of arbitration, some form of decision, should take the place of the strike. I believe that the steps toward resolving this problem will only be taken through discussion, education and understanding; they will not be taken through legislation or dictation. Above all, the solution will not be found if we adopt what some so readily talk about. When some talk about compulsory arbitration they really mean that they want a solution for low wages rather than fair wages. Far too often that is the solution some people want. I will have no part of any solution to take the place of a strike that is not fair, because I know that working men originally went on strike in protest against conditions which were unfair. The strike weapon was the weapon they chose, illegal though it was, in their search for fair dealing. We should bear these considerations in mind in any search for solutions.
In no jurisdiction of this country has the solution to this problem been found easy or simple. Given our present system of labour-management relations, there is not any province in this country which has not experienced difficulty in resolving labour disputes, in bringing about solutions. Men charged with the responsibility of government in this country earnestly try to find solutions to labour problems. On the other hand the opposition says, "Let us march in and settle a strike right away." It says that simply because it need not put forward alternative solutions, because it need not suggest how we will bring about, step by step, conditions which will lead to the labour peace, which is so essential to this country.

Actually our record over the years has been extremely good. It is our competitors who like to put forward the contrary view. That does not mean we are over our difficulties in this area. I ask hon. members opposite if they are responsible to speak about alternatives to the kind of collective bargaining process we have in this country, or alternatives to the legitimate strike weapon. Neither the Conservative government of Ontario nor any other Conservative jurisdiction in this country has found an easy and facile solution to the problem. That is a fact. I ask leadership candidates opposite, or those who like to make late night speeches, to make suggestions in this area instead of sounding a note of alarm.
I found it amazing to note one or two of them taking the credit for the settlement of the dispute, although some were fair enough to give credit to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) who so richly deserves credit for the long hours he has spent working on this matter. Too often, when discussions are going on, the government has to remain silent and not interfere with negotiations, while the opposition comes forward with its interventions, talk and irrelevancies. That is behind us.
When the President of the Treasury Board rose to announce the settlement of the strike, I noticed the looks of sadness which came over the faces of some opposition members who were disappointed at the strike settlement for some short-sighted tactical reason. We must give credit to the President of the Treasury Board, and we must embark on discussions which will lead to positive suggestions on how to resolve difficult labour-management relations. We must bring about a legitimate form of settlement, one that does not impose poor conditions and low wages on the working men of this country.

I am standing here on behalf of the Canadian people who want leadership in times of industrial disruption. I recall my seatmate indicating he was concerned about the paramountcy of the public interest. Certainly we have appreciation for the collective bargaining process and the time-honoured right to strike and lock-out. But there must come a time when the public's interest is overriding and when the necessary steps to preserve it must be taken. That is why hon. members are sitting over there temporarily; it is to give leadership in that regard.
In the past several months Canada has been the victim of a succession of strikes affecting the movement of grain. This is what disturbs us. This is what, I am sure, disturbs members on the other side of the House. They know that as a result of these strikes Canada's international reputation is being ruined. They know Canada has suffered economically. Need I remind them again of the 222 grain
March 19, 1975

inspectors? We hope the longshoremen will settle. Apparently the grain weighers and the samplers have settled.
What will be the consequences of these stoppages? Well, between 30 and 40 vessels are waiting in Vancouver. Some 90 shipping days have been lost. Canada is now 900,000 tons behind in grain deliveries to China from both coasts. China is now negotiating to buy one million tons of grain for 1975, and the delays I have mentioned have jeopardized this. Japan is replacing March, April and some May grain shipments by negotiating purchases from the United States and Australia. There are 22,000 boxcars sitting out on the prairies. Yet the minister says this is a little strike. This shows a callous disregard for the welfare of the Canadian people as well as for our international obligations.
What about demurrage? Members opposite play this down. The word simply means fees paid to ship owners to compensate for delays. These fees are paid ultimately by the farmers; the figure has already reached some $17 million and, as has been stated by my hon. friend from Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), it could yet reach between $35 million and $40 million. Let me give you the facts, Mr. Speaker. We deal in facts on this side; we don't deal with hanky panky.
In 1971-72 demurrage fees amounted to $1,871,000. For 1972-73, the figure was $2,397,636. In 1973-74 it was $17 million. Yet the President of the Treasury Board has the gall to talk about a little strike. The effect of this strike has been damaging to the Canadian economy. Future grain markets have been jeopardized. It is time we began to take notice of where we are going. We have heard all about the collective bargaining process. We have heard all about voluntary arbitration and compulsory arbitration. All I know is that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) had better get going with his consultative process between labour, management and governments in an effort to come up with a solution.

I have lost my voice today, but I have been waiting to say this for so long that I intend to say it, whether you can hear me or not. Prince Rupert has been a port for 65 years, but became a national harbour in reality only on March 1 of this year, when the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) jumped into an earth mover and turned the first sod on federal general cargo facilities in that port. It will not be too long before vessels finally learn that Prince Rupert is 500 miles closer to the Orient than Vancouver. This constitutes a saving to shipping of one day's sailing.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, the north has grain to ship. But this country is not only grain, and I hope the members from the prairies in this chamber can hear me. Grain is not the only commodity we can talk about in this country. We have large resources of pulp and wood products, aluminium and copper concentrates, molybdenum, silver, jade, halibut and herring, fertilizer, and even the occasional manufactured goods manage to get shipped from our port. No, Mr. Speaker, Canada is not just grain, and neither is the west coast of B.C. Always, as in the motion before us tonight, it is grain of which the members of the House speak.
Through arbitration and mediation, through hard bargaining by labour and management as well as the government, we find at last an agreement. What do the people of B.C. say-the miners, fishermen, loggers and mill workers? They say, "What about us? What about our products? Don't we count just as much as the grain farmers? Isn't our contribution to the economy of this country just as important as theirs?"
The man who loads the primary products at northern British Columbia ports is just as much valued. He has to suffer a differential in his living that is practically

unknown to those who live below the 53rd parallel in this country. He suffers a differential in amenities that other Canadians take for granted. His wage negotiations do not reflect the north-south division of this nation's wealth. His children have less access to education, they have fewer dentists, fewer doctors, fewer teachers and fewer professional people of all types.
The holidaying southern Canadian takes off from his home and goes 100 miles, gets in an airplane and flies away. We have to drive a thousand miles at times to get an airplane, which costs a good deal more as the distance is a good deal greater. Do you see compensation in their wage settlements for that? I suggest that you do not.
You often see southern dominated unions putting men on a northern differential or on a regional wage, but you find that often the special allowances are cancelled as a result of agreements by the unions as well as by management. Apparently these few northerners do not matter.
It is the same way when grain vessels are delayed by the process of negotiation. We then hear that all the products I have mentioned really do not matter. All the talk is then about grain. The suggestion is that we should settle the grain movement and everything will be all right. I admit that grain is very important to this country and this country would be nowhere without it, but I ask you to consider and remember that grain is not synonymous with Canada, just as Vancouver and the west coast are not synonymous with Canada.
The utilization of northern ports so much closer to Asian markets must be considered for all or a major part of new storage and handling facilities.
