subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I only wish there were more participants from the Liberal side like the hon. member who has just resumed her seat. Her speech will read well to the prairie farmers who have become angered and aggravated by the inactivity of the government. I think that when they read her speech, with a sprinkling of the others that have been made tonight, they will realize that members of parliament have a tough job here as Conservatives, particularly those from the prairies, when we have this type of attitude to buck.
The hon. lady spoke as though grain were the only thing we were concerned about. That is not the only thing we are concerned about, but it so happens that on this particular occasion there was a public service strike of blue collar workers. This was a rotating strike, but for some reason or other the only segment that did not rotate was the grain handlers' segment. It is significant for members of the opposition to point that fact out to the hon. lady and other Liberals who were not aware of the fact that the only segment that did not rotate was the grain handlers.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, tried to parley this thing into a great conflict. He tried to make the House think there were actually two strikes in Canada at this time, and that there had been two strikes all along. The grain weighers and samplers have been effectively on strike since February 7, whereas the longshoremen have only been on strike for the past week or so.
The Minister of Justice spoke about what one must consider as the national interest, and he suggested that solutions must be fair. He said that above all Canada must remain a dependable supplier. I would ask the hon. minister to take into consideration what is in the national interest. Back on August 31, 1972, the government brought in Bill C-231 in recognition of the fact that the national interest was being endangered by the longshoremen on the west coast who should be put back to work. That bill dealt with that strike. The then Minister of Labour, now the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell), had this to say when introducing that bill:
But there are occasions when parliament must deal with situations, when the full resort to economic warfare by strike or lockout so impairs the ability of others to carry on their activities that it can be said to be against the national interest-
The Liberals do recognize that, at times when economic warfare carried on by strike does impair the ability of others to carry out their activities, this affects national interest. That was on August 31, 1972, and is history. We have to determine now what is in the national interest.
We are concerned when Canada imports far more than it exports. We realize that our exports play an important part in allowing Canada to meet its balance of payments in order that we can continue to enjoy our standard of living. In a recent document by the Bank of Canada, namely, its annual report for 1974, we find this statement: A good deal will depend on what happens abroad, for Canada cannot be expected to regain its economic health and vigour without an upturn in economic activity in the United States and in other important markets for Canadian exports.
The entire report, particularly the first 10 pages, suggests that Canada's exports are of vital importance to our wellbeing. The striking grain weighers number 40 people.
Grain Shipments
We had to bring about a settlement that is fair to them and in the national interest. Those 40 people have tied up the grain movement for better than four weeks. We have to weigh the rights of those 40 people against the harm they have done to the total economy.
There is an interesting point which has not been referred to tonight, and I should like the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) to listen and learn a little bit about grain. When grain is sold on long-term contracts it is priced at the time of delivery. We have been experiencing a falling market, and grain prices have dropped $1.50 since January 1. Some members of this House, even on the government side, have suggested that we have lost 50 million bushels in sales. We have lost well over $50 million on the sales we should have been making. Those 40 people tied up the movement of grain and cost the prairie farmers well over $200 million when you total up the loss of sales, the demurrage charges and the depreciating price of grain.
It is interesting to note the following which appeared in the Globe and Mail of February 25, 1975:
Canada has the grain, said Mr. Lang. The question is: 'How easily can we get the farmers to deliver it'?
The whole article encourages farmers to deliver grain. Then we have these headlines which appeared in the
Financial Post for March 15:
Strikes force Wheat Board to Discourage Grain Planting.
I am reading merely the headline. Certainly some people thought the national interest was affected. What made them think that? How did they reach that conclusion? In the 33 weeks since the current crop year began, for 11 weeks grain shipments have been held up. There have been only two occasions since August of 1973 when there has not been a tie-up of ships at the Vancouver port. No one can suggest that that is a smooth handling system when one realizes there have been only two occasions when ships have not been tied up, and when there has not been a backlog at the port of Vancouver.
Mr. Harrold, chairman of the Wheat Board Advisory Committee and President of the Alberta Wheat Pool, said that the board may be forced to limit future sales through west coast ports to 20 million bushels a month or less. The average movement in the past few years has been 30 million bushels a month. Mr. Turner, the president of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, says that prairie grain movement is the worst in the past four years. One of the largest grain handling agencies on the prairies says that the grain movement is the worst it has been in the past four years.
Surely it should be apparent to almost everybody that it is in the national interest for us in this House of Commons to urge some kind of action on the part of the government, not only in settling the strike which apparently has been settled but, if necessary, not to hesitate for another four weeks to settle the strike which may or may not be voted on tomorrow. One could go on and on in this regard. We note from the Globe and Mail of March 18 that 82 vessels must wait a minimum of three more days because of the strike at Vancouver. Certainly that is the largest armada that has been gathered in any port since World War II.

Admittedly only 40 of those vessels may be engaged in carrying wheat or grain because the other 42 may be involved in carrying containers, lumber, and some of the other things mentioned by the hon. member for Skeena. Surely this must constitute some need for government action. One of the largest ships has been there for over a month waiting for grain to be loaded. This is grain destined for Bangladesh which is badly in need of food. In fact thousands of people are starving in that country. Surely it is in the national interest for the opposition to be concerned about this matter.
I notice the members of the other opposition parties have been pretty silent. There are no members of the New Democratic Party in the House. We are working overtime and perhaps they are not getting paid for overtime. Most of the time they profess to be the great saviours for the starving people throughout the world. Were they concerned about that vessel being held up? Apparently they were not. Not one of them has spoken in this debate tonight. They have all gone home. Is this an indication of how much interest they have in the welfare of the farmers or the plight of the starving people throughout the world? It is only a quarter to eleven. Quite often we work this late. I am shocked that they would leave so early and take no part in this debate. They are not concerned about the national interest. They are not concerned about the starving people of Bangladesh or the tie-up on the west coast. They are only interested in their political well-being, which has been severely shocked.

While this is madness in a world beset by energy shortages and hunger, such strikes are exceedingly dangerous for Canadians. The closing of the ports for the fifth time in 10 years is very effectively scuppering Canada's reputation as a reliable supplier-
Then there is reference to page 12 where there is a lengthy argument on the subject. Certainly one could quote articles day in and day out on this subject. Now I should like to quote from the Free Press Weekly for March 15, 1975. It states:
Forrest Hetland, commissioner with the Canadian Grain Commission, may have best expressed sentiments throughout the grains industry when he said, "I am the most depressed person in all Canada today".
"Canada's reputation has gone down, down, down ... it's the worst it's ever been since I've been here.
It's a God-awful situation".
I believe he was appointed six years ago. That is what a commissioner appointed by the minister said. He must have thought there was a national issue here. He must have thought the country was affected by it because he spoke out loud and clear, even though he was a civil servant handling and grading grain for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) who is in charge of the Wheat Board. I do not know what kind of justice the minister hands out and to whom he deals it out, but it was certainly not justice to the prairie farmers on this occasion.
The article then reads:
Canadian Wheat Board offices were deluged with messages from countries that could no longer accept apologies from the central marketing agency-
The Canadian Wheat Board is the central marketing agency for farmers' grain and they have become a very respected agency throughout the world. But this is what they said on March 5, and I am reading from the March 15
issue of the Free Press Weekly:
-grain orders and incoming ships were diverted from the paralysed port of Vancouver-
I cannot imagine why the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) has not expressed concern. I know she is a member representing the northern part of British Columbia, but surely the antagonism between the north
March 19, 1975

and the south of British Columbia is not so great that she cannot share part of the responsibility and concern for the southern part of that province. The Wheat Board said, further:
-Japanese shipping firms attempted to pull their ships out of Vancouver but were blocked by picket lines, and spokesmen for large, international trading houses in New York called Canada's performance "just unbelievable".
I think, also, there are many prairie farmers who believe that this government's performance is just unbelievable. I am very pleased that we on this side of the House initiated this debate, and because of that we can take some credit for spurring on a settlement of a strike which has lasted five full weeks. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board asked what alternatives the opposition has. It seems to me that the Liberal bank of ideas has run dry. It is they who are in power; they are supposed to have all the facts. My friend here says they had lots of promises in July. Yes, they seemed to have; but we on this side of the House realize that those promises were hollow.
They even had a transportation policy. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board was going to do away with the Crowsnest pass rates, but now the government realizes that with an election coming up in Saskatchewan it should not try to eliminate them. So the minister shelved this proposal and told the Saskatchewan people that the Crowsnest pass rates are here to stay for all of 1975. This is the great reassurance which they give in the hope they will win another election.
The minister asks, what are the alternatives? I have already said that many people, many marketing agencies and government officials in charge of handling Canadian grain believe that the national interest has been, and is being, affected by the inactivity of this government. A settlement must be fair. In this case, 40 employees tied up the whole western economy for five weeks. This is hardly fair. The government should have acted long before it did. It is hardly fair that there can be a rotating strike of airport workers, a rotating strike of snow removal crews, but not a rotating strike of grain weighers. They wanted to affect the largest possible segment of the economy because they wanted action from somebody. They had to wait a long time to get action from this government.
I believe that an alternative would be to establish a labour settlement commission which would attempt to settle a strike prior to the expiry of a contract. We do not have to wait until everyone is on strike before we realize that somebody will be out of work if we do not get them back to work. Surely we are educated enough to be able to communicate with one another prior to the expiry date of a contract. The labour settlement commission could bring in a report and the matter could be settled in time. Parliament would know whether that settlement was satisfactory and whether there would be a legal or an illegal strike.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose it is usual or traditional in certain circumstances to begin one's remarks with a reference to being pleased to take part in a debate, or words of that kind. In fact, I have
Grain Shipments
used those expressions myself on occasion. But I am not pleased at having to take part in this discussion this evening, and I doubt if many hon. members can really say they are pleased to be here discussing this particular subject. This is not because the subject is unimportant-it is vitally important-and it is not because we are unhappy with the settlement that, fortunately, was reached earlier today, because we are delighted with the success of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) in that respect, but we are not happy with the procedure this evening because, once again, we find ourselves dangerously close to a situation where parliament might be called upon to legislate the conclusion of an industrial dispute. That would be a most unhappy turn of events which I do not think any member of this House would welcome.
We have heard tonight, from other hon. members, some of the kinds of damage which these disputes involving the Public Service Alliance of Canada, the Treasury Board and the longshoremen on the west coast have caused- damage such as demurrage charges which farmers will have to bear, damage such as lost opportunities to make sales during the time of the shut-down, damage possibly to our reputation as a reliable grain supplier, the congestion which is now in our system and which may take some time to unclog, deferred contracts and the problem of a large carry-over at the end of the year. Those are real problems which are particularly acute for the western grain producers who, I am happy to say, are represented in great numbers in the constituency of Assiniboia which I have the honour to represent in this House.
Let me tell the House of a statement which was prepared this afternoon by the board of directors of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. The preamble to that statement is most important because it expresses the attitude of concern in western Canada. The board of directors said:
Provincewide anger and frustration over strikes in Canada are growing in intensity as farmers see clearly the devastating effects labour disputes have on our whole economy. We have been holding numerous public meetings throughout the province and these have been attended by thousands of farmers and numerous non-farmers as well. At every single meeting deep concern has been expressed about Canada's labour situation particularly with the disputes that have virtually stopped the flow of grain out of the country. Lost sales means lost revenue to farmers and other sectors of the economy.
That is a portion of what the board of directors had to say this afternoon in reference to the particular problem which was, fortunately, settled earlier today. It is an important expression of opinion because in this country we have a tremendous problem. I hazard to suggest that the matter of labour-management negotiations and industrial dispute settlements is probably the biggest challenge facing all levels of government federal, provincial and municipal as well as the private sector for at least the next year and a half. We are not happy that this challenge is again before the nation and this parliament. We are fortunate to have tonight a final settlement of the Public Service Alliance dispute, and hopefully within 48 hours we will have a final settlement with the longshoremen.
I want to devote a few minutes to the topic I spoke about some time ago in this House and which I know caught the attention of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) who initiated the discussion this

March 19, 1975
Grain Shipments
evening. I refer to a remark I made during my first speech in this House. That was last October, on the occasion when the House of Commons was considering the grain handlers' dispute in Vancouver. At that time I said, and I will repeat it tonight, that there must be a better answer and let us work to find that better way. The crucial issue is just that: what is the better way; what is the alternative?

speechtext: What is the better way?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES
speechtext:
I welcome the interjection by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) on that point. We are all striving to achieve a better way. We hear few real answers from hon. members opposite other than sloganeering and critical harangues. Others could be more helpful in putting forward positive ideas. That is what the efforts now under way to reach a reasonable, national consensus on this issue are all about. That is what the Finkleman report is all about. That is what the Bayda commission in Vancouver is all about, and that is what the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool was all about this afternoon when its board of directors made the statement I read earlier. I would like to read the concluding sentence from that statement:
-we would welcome the calling of a general conference of government, labour and industry representatives to determine the means to improve the collective bargaining process in Canada.
I would like to associate myself with the sentiments expressed earlier this evening by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) when he called for the quest for an alternate system of dispute settlement which would not simply outlaw the right to strike by making it illegal or simply removing it. That is a rather simple solution which just will not work. Rather, we must develop what he referred to as a credible and effective mechanism which will render the strike weapon unnecessary. Simply rendering strikes illegal will not solve the problem; we must go to the root and render them unnecessary.
I would like to offer a specific proposal which I hope will commend itself to members of this House and to the government. I ask that we immediately seek out all parties which have any effect on or association with the grain handling industry-because it is a sensitive and very important industry-and seek from them a specific and concrete agreement and undertaking. Perhaps we can propose to the industry that grain handling be a special case or a test case. I think the expression of opinion this afternoon from the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool might be an indication that the parties in the grain industry would be willing to go along with such a suggestion. In a concentrated effort we could, with good will on both sides, without sloganeering, politicking or haranguing, experiment with alternate forms of dispute settlement over a specific period of time.
We would have a genuine national experiment with other ways of dispute settlement so that we would not be confronted with work stoppages. We would achieve agreement on that matter at the outset and then work with alternate methods. We could offer our farmers and customers greater assurance that "the grain will in fact go through." Our experience with grain could lead the way to a new regime. This experiment could point the way to a new establishment which would be a credible and realistic
alternative in which both sides to a dispute could have confidence, in which the public could have confidence and in which we could all place our faith and trust so that damaging work stoppages in the future would be seen to
be unnecessary.
As I say, and as other hon. members on this side of the House have said this evening-I hope the sentiment is general, and I suspect that it is despite some of the superficial comments to the contrary-it is not good enough to write some fancy slogan or punitive law on the wall and say, "Thou shalt not strike," because strikes will occur and they will be that much more difficult to deal with because they will be illegal strikes. We have to find the consensus, the basic foundation of opinion so we can find a way to make strikes, not necessarily illegal but very definitely unnecessary in this country so that work stoppages which damage so many other innocent people will be unnecessary.
I hope this suggestion will commend itself to hon. members of this House and I hope we can make use of the very sensitive and important grain industry as a place to start that great experiment.

speechtext: I am pleased, however, to see that two of the Liberal representatives from the province of Saskatchewan are interested enough in this debate and in the handling of grain to be in attendance tonight. This tie-up of grain is of great concern to all farmers in the west and to all businessmen. Indeed, it is an important matter as far as the whole economy of our country is concerned. I recall coming back last fall after the election and participating in the debate on Bill C-12 which legislated the grain handlers back to work. I re-read the speech which I gave at that time-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES
speechtext:
I did enjoy it, but I felt sad. I found in the speech at page 218 of Hansard a quotation from the Globe and Mail Report on Business for Friday, October 4, 1974. This is what it said:
Japan has been forced to buy spot cargoes of wheat at a premium from the United States because of the six-week old grain handlers' strike in Vancouver, according to the Canadian Wheat Board.
The board said yesterday that the amounts of wheat Japan was forced to buy amounted to hundreds of thousands of tons.
The grain handlers' strike would have caused even more damage to Canada's reputation as a reliable exporter but for the fact there is so little available grain in the world that importers have had to stick with this country.
If the Board were concerned about Canada's reputation as a grain exporter in October, 1974, what is its feeling today? Agriculture is one of Canada's most important industries. It is the lifeblood of every community in the prairie provinces, and it has a great effect on the balance of payments. There is a spinoff to every other industry in Canada, machinery manufacturing in the east, automobile manufacturing, truck manufacturing and many other things. It is an industry that is persistently plagued with strikes.
Since the beginning of the crop year, August 1, 1974, the port of Vancouver has been shut down 35 per cent of the time. We have defaulted on contracts and have been called upon to pay penalties to the importing countries. The amount of these penalties are not known and the producer may never know them.
On Tuesday, March 11, I put the following question to the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board which appears at page 3976 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. On March 3 I asked the minister whether delays in moving grain on the west coast had resulted in Canada being called upon to pay sums of money under the penalty clauses in contracts entered into for the sale of grain, and the minister said he would look into the matter on an up to date basis. Is he now in a position to give an up to date answer?
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, needless to say, there are many contracts and the details are rather voluminous. The matter is also a very complex legal one. Perhaps it might be amenable to a discussion between the hon. member and myself, which I am prepared to have at this time.
I had a discussion with the minister two days later and he said that there were problems; that we had been called upon to pay penalties to some of the importing countries under our contract. He said it was a rather ticklish matter and a complex situation. He said that if he were to tell me
Grain Shipments
and the House the amount of these penalties it would prejudice our position as a grain exporter. I appreciate that fact, Mr. Speaker, and I would not want to see our position prejudiced. But at some point, Mr. Speaker, the grain producer in Canada is entitled to know what this tie-up of grain by the strike has cost him.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
At least $40 million. And what about lost sales? I am sure we will never know the extent of our lost sales in the last few months. I know the Americans are picking up sales as a result of our default. The report of the National Association of Wheat Growers dated March 7, 1975, in Washington has this to say:
Canadian grain movement has been completely halted by grain handler strikes at government elevators and a walk-out by west coast longshoremen. Canada is already way behind in meeting scheduled export shipments, and the continuing labour disputes have caused a back up of 20,000 loaded grain cars at west coast ports and idled over 30 vessels at Vancouver, B.C.
Shifts to U.S. wheat will be one significant result of the Canadian difficulties, and western wheat associates announced this week that Japan will purchase an additional six million bushels of U.S. wheat for shipment during March-April because of the tie-up.
There is another aspect of the tie-up, Mr. Speaker. There are indications that certain importing countries will be calling upon us to deliver grain through eastern Canadian ports. A recent newspaper report indicates that the most recent contract that China has with Canada calls for 40 per cent of that contract to be delivered through eastern Canadian ports. I tried to find out from the minister if other countries were requiring similar delivery arrangements, and I put the following question to him yesterday as recorded at page 4200 of Hansard:
Apart from the decision of the government of China to insist on deliveries of 40 per cent of its recent contract through the eastern ports, have other customers recently required that a portion of their grain shipments be sent through the eastern ports?
The minister answered:
The story about China having required delivery of 40 per cent of its supplies through eastern ports was inaccurate.
The minister did not answer my question, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps the figure of 40 per cent is not accurate, but what is the figure? What other countries are calling upon Canada to deliver grain through ports other than the port of Vancouver? The producer is entitled to know this.
I was interested in a report which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen on February 26, 1975, headlined "The port of Vancouver will die ..The article quotes Mr. Fred Spoke, manager of the port of Vancouver, as saying:
The port of Vancouver, biggest grain outlet in the world has "a grave obligation to a needy and hungry world ... it should be allowed to live up to its stature."
He went on to say:
Buyers are getting very apprehensive... and it's about time the public raised its voice. It's a horrendous situation, incredible. The

Grain Shipments
United Kingdom used to be considered the worst country for labour relations-now we've apparently stolen the crown from them.
Then he said:
We have very, very good facilities to export commodities, the presence of the Amoco is proof of that, but we have never been able to live up to our capacity because of circumstances beyond our control.
The article contains another interesting statement made by Mr. Stanley Reid, president of the central division of the Canadian International Freight Forwarders Association, who said:
The port of Vancouver, I don't think there's any doubt, will die.
What happens if the port of Vancouver dies? What will it mean to grain producers? Mr. Speaker, it will mean higher transportation costs on the export of grain to the Pacific rim countries. It will mean lower prices and smaller incomes for producers. It will mean that our deliveries of export grain are limited to the period during which the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence waterway system is open, and during the time the Churchill system is open.
The producers of grain are in a strange situation. They are paid the initial price and then wait a year for the final payment. The producer has no control over what the final payment will be. He does not control the movement of grain, its export price, or the handling and export costs. Those are factors beyond his control.
Strikes take place with great frequency in the grain handling business, but the producer cannot do anything about them. He takes no part in collective bargaining, yet pays the increased costs when collective bargaining has been finalized. He pays the cost of penalties resulting from breach of contract, and pays costs of demurrage. He is simply a pawn.
As I said, agriculture is the most important industry in Canada. If we are to have a viable industry and viable economy, it must remain one of the leading industries in Canada. Before entering the House this evening I read again the speeches of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and of the Minister of Labour, made in October last year when this House settled the grain handlers' strike. I found it interesting to note that the ministers in both those speeches simply recited the history of the strike, and not once did they mention that the strike was being settled because it was in the national interest. According to all indications, the settlement was politically expedient. The government had decided that the time had come to settle the strike, and it settled it on grounds of political expediency.
To me the national interest is all-important. While I believe in the inalienable right of workers to strike-

-I think the public interest is more important than the right to strike. We cannot let strikes upset our economy and create chaos.
Apparently the west coast strike has been settled, but I anticipate further problems in the immediate future. Certainly in this enlightened day and age we should resolve our labour disputes without resorting to strikes. We must

invite the government, industry and labour to co-operate and arrive at a solution.
Ours is a great country. Canada is one of the finest countries in the world. Wa must solve the problem of strikes and labour unrest; otherwise we will destroy our country.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened carefully to members on the government side and members of the official opposition, I could not help sympathizing with them. When they find the economic system they believe in and support collapsing around their ears, they immediately seek scapegoats.
If you are a Liberal or Conservative member from an urban centre, you blame those darned farmers; if you are a Liberal or Conservative member from the prairies, you blame those darned labourers. You know, this reminds me of the days of the kings, the dukes, the lords and the czars. Their motto was, divide and rule. If you keep different groups fighting each other you will rule them, you can win elections, or win enough seats to form the official opposition or be the government. You can speak out of both sides of your mouth, or speak with forked tongues. Such people speak with hot mouths but cold hearts. They have been doing this since 1867.
I admire the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campag-nolo) for saying what she said. I sympathize with her. The ailment with her voice, although I did not tell her, is an ailment common to people in our occupation. It is known as preacher's throat. The only known cure is keeping your mouth shut-but she and I have failed in this. If the hon. member for Skeena would address the remarks she made tonight, which I thought were excellent, to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and to the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan, I should be most grateful, as would be all the farmers and workers in Saskatchewan. If she would do that she would do a great service for industrial peace in western Canada, if nowhere else.
Members on the government side, members of the opposition, of my party and of the Creditiste party should look at what our society has done for decades, that is, at how we treat people with high incomes as opposed to how we treat people with low incomes. I ask the hon. member for Skeena, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), and the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mcl-saac) to consider why employees of the government of Canada, that is, of the people of Canada, who earn low incomes are acting as they are. Let them consider what causes strikes.
Who are the people who go on strike. Well, they are ordinary people. They have wives, children and mortgages up to their eyebrows. They see that the government allows deputy ministers, assistant deputy ministers and executive assistants, whose Ph.D. thesis was on the sex life of the date Palm, salary increases ranging from $6,000 to $10,000 a year. These were granted without bargaining. A union was not involved. Actually I don't know if the people concerned even asked for as much as they got. But the Treasury Board, the hon. member for Skeena, the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley acquiesced in those increases. Those people were given increases equivalent to what some of
March 19, 1975

the people on strike in Canada earn in a whole year. If hon. members opposite wonder why government employees disobey the law, let them bear in mind the hypocrisy of the government which says that if your income is high, your salary shall be increased by $8,000 or $10,000 a year, and you will be paid even more for overtime. Executive assistants are to be paid money on top of their increases for overtime.
On the other hand the man who cleans the airport runway, or samples grain or weighs grain, is to get an increase that does not even allow him to catch up with the increased cost of living brought about by inflation. People like that are the first victims of this so-called free enterprise society you all advocate, and you wonder why they will not stand for it.

May I return to the point I made earlier and quote a world-famous historical figure.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES
speechtext: Was that Abe Lincoln?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES
speechtext:
That is what he said the second time he ran for the Senate. I urge my hon. friend behind the curtain to read about Abraham Lincoln, who said that without labour capital cannot function.
If those of my hon. friends in this House really believe in the free enterprise system and want to make it function, they had better listen to someone like Abraham Lincoln. He was 100 years ahead of some of the members who sit in this House. Every time I listen to some of my friends in the Conservative and Liberal parties I feel they are trying to prove Karl Marx was right when he said capitalism will destroy itself. For 100 years in Canada both the Liberal and Conservative parties have been trying to prove that he was right. They still seem to think that the owners and proprietors of capital have the final and only say about how people shall earn their living. They do not even want to prevent a totalitarian system. Some of the remarks that I heard this evening could be attributed to Mussolini in the 1920's.
I know that some of my friends in the Conservative and Liberal parties in the House are as good or better democrats than I am, but let them be careful and think about what they say. Do not pay lip service to collective bargaining and the right to strike. Do not play upon the fears, worries and hardships of the farmers at the expense of the workers. This does not do any favour to any decent, civilized society.
Whether any of us win or lose elections is not the point. What counts is the contribution we make here to resolving our problems. At the rate we are going the difficulties we have had over the past few months are going to get worse, 
but we have an opportunity tonight and over the next two or three weeks to take some action.
The government does not need to ask the members of the opposition what ideas they have because we have given them to the government lots of times. I am not saying we are 100 per cent right, no one is 100 per cent right-or wrong for that matter. I remind the hon. member for Skeena that she should get in touch with the leader of the Liberal party of Saskatchewan and get him to keep his big mouth shut in order to make a good contribution to the settlement of industrial strife in this country. That would be very helpful. You cannot have Liberals in Saskatchewan saying one thing and Liberals in Ottawa saying something else.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the late hour and so as not to give too heavy a load to the employees of the House of Commons, I shall cut short the comments that I had intended to make during this debate.
However, I am convinced that the chair acted wisely this afternoon in allowing tonight's debate. First of all, this gave us the opportunity to witness an excellent procedural debate which was, in my opinion, most interesting, and which can inspire us in the future in a similar situation.
Despite the announcement that the conflict is settled, the chair allowed this debate to be held. This is evidence of the great freedom which exists in this institution. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) is not in his seat, and I understand him, and still congratulate him for having settled the conflict. I hope that the settlement will not be temporary but lasting. I give him the credit he deserves because when the minister is not successful, he is charged with not having done his job. As he has been successful today, I believe that we should tell him to use the same formula to settle the other conflicts which exist in our country and greatly perturb our economy.
The official opposition, on the other hand, congratulates itself for having forced the government to act more quickly. I am convinced that the opposition is right because the role of members of Parliament is to be interested in all the problems and the whole administration of our country. In our institution, some members sit on the government side and others on the opposition side. I believe that every member, on whatever side he sits, if he does his job and is really interested in the affairs of his country, greatly helps the government administer the affairs of Canada.
I have always believed and I am ever more convinced, Mr. Speaker, that inflation is at the root of many ills in Canada, that it gives rise to work stoppages because the workers do not have a sufficient income to meet their commitments. So they ask for higher wages because prices have risen, and because prices have risen the workers again ask for better wages because the cost of living has gone up. I do not believe that this is a solution. If it were,
March 19, 1975

we would have solved our problems long ago. But one senses that the situation is worsening day by day. If one compares the figures provided by Statistics Canada on gross national product for the year 1974, in constant dollars, that represents $139 billion today, but in comparison with 1961 it is only $69 billion. That is a typical example of what inflation can do. That information comes from Statistics Canada.
Getting back directly to the motion, if the copy I have in my hand is correct, it reads: "The present work stoppages which have ended all grain shipments from Canada affecting grain deliveries to all foreign countries, creating increasing unemployment." I am convinced that is also true because all work stoppages check economic activity in several sectors. Industries feel the effects, layoffs increase, and automatically the whole economy of our country is affected. It goes on: "The loss of orders of grain and the grave potential for the loss of foreign grain customers generally."
I listened carefully earlier to the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) who spoke strongly about the merits of western grain producers and their problems. I congratulate him on that, and I agree with what he said. I too admit that western grain producers contribute for a large part to the gross national product of this country, the increase in the standard of living of Canadians, and also to helping those countries which lack food and whose populations are starving. Thanks to our very productive soil and western grain producers Canada can afford to help developing countries so they can survive and continue to develop. In Canada, there is another area known as the east. Parliament must deal with the problems of western Canada; it has the duty to do so, but it must also be concerned about those of eastern Canada. In the east, there is now a conflict that affects the movement of feed grains towards the east, and which is of great concern to the producers of that area. I brought this situation to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) yesterday. I have received many telegrams. Here is one, among others:
Feed grain situation precarious-Limited quantities in Quebec elevators-Certain shortage within ten days unless blue-collar strike settled-Request immediate settlement.
In other words, those producers are asking their member of parliament to point out the problems to this House. That is what I am doing and I hope the ministers will take this situation into account. I therefore urge the President of the Treasury Board to use the same recipe that solved the conflict in Vancouver, that Canada's eastern producers not suffer too much from the conflict.
If grains are not brought in sufficient quantities to the elevators of eastern Canada, people will fight to get grain at any price; production costs are going to increase, which may easily drive pork producers out of business, resulting in the same kind of bankruptcies as last year or two years ago.
Madam Speaker, if I insisted on informing the House and the government of the-kind of situation which prevails in eastern Canada, it is because it is directly related to what happens now in western Canada. And if a settle-
Grain Shipments
ment was reached, I think the same efforts should be made to find a solution to the work stoppage which paralyzes grain movements before it is too late. I heard moments ago members saying with reason that problems are left to aggravate, thus making it difficult to solve them. I am perfectly aware that governing no longer is a sinecure today. It is not easy either, with the current spirit among people, with all those invitations, on the right and on the left, to demonstrate, sometimes with reason, but sometimes also unreasonably. People seem to be willing to demonstrate for demonstrating is sake, therefore upsetting managers and leading them really sometimes to wonder whether people are acting seriously or not. That is why it has become increasingly difficult to manage. Therefore, the government and Parliament must be much more careful than ever. They must always be on the look out for possible conflicts to try and locate them right from the beginning in order to bring in solutions before the situation gets worse. I think that is the way Canadians immag-ine the Canadian Parliament, trying to find means of avoiding the worst and solving problems which they could not avoid. I think this is the working pattern we should consider in Parliament, whatever party we belong to. Moments ago I heard the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) wondering about the silence of members who sit in this part of the House, Social Credit members. I shall tell him this: We cannot all talk together, we have to wait until we get the floor. He can be sure that we from eastern Canada are deeply concerned by all the problems occurring in the west, because we are interdependent in Parliament. We have the same responsibilities toward the people of the west as those in the east. Such is my position, this is how I have always seen things and I will continue to see them. I want mutual respect to exist both east and west.
Owing to the serious conditions and the meetings which eastern members have held in recent days with milk producers, we note that they seem dissatisfied and justly so, because production costs are increasing. They feel compelled to ask again the government to adjust the price of manufacturing milk at the level of production costs.
In my opinion, to avoid another problem, we shall have to take necessary measures to meet their demands. I am not one of those who are scared by threats and I have never been taken in by them. But it did not take me long at those meetings to realize that producers have serious problems they are unable to solve. They need the help of the government and they need it badly to know the contents of the new government policy which will take effect next April 1.
Having analysed with them the production costs, I think their demands of $11.60 per hundred weight are totally justified. At the same time, I should like to make a very practical proposal to the government, so as not to overburden consumers, low income families and workers who in most cases already have too much to pay.
There was once in Canada a policy of butter subsidy. I had that experience and benefited from it like other people my age. Well, if this policy was good then, I wonder why it should not be good now. Yet, such formulas must be used, so that some part of the population is not penalized at the expense of another. Producers and consumers will have to learn to live together and stop fighting and

March 19, 1975
Grain Shipments
accusing each other. They will have to get to understand one another better. Parliament will also have to assume its responsibilities and discover what is going on among the middlemen, in the big outfits, those we do not know but who are quite active, so as to find out how they can manage to fleece both the consumers and producers at the same time. Such is the function of government. I already talked about this and I say it again tonight: so long as we will not have the courage to go and see what is going on in that segment of our economy, we shall see problems getting worse, dissatisfied consumers, ill-paid producers, and a government embarrassed and uncertain about the course to take.
In my opinion, the government would be well advised to create a commission to examine what is going on in that sanctuary. Its members would not be appointed on a political basis, but would be qualified, honest, persons who would be able to go to the heart of problems and to report to the government. Members should then have enough courage to pass legislation to implement the reports produced.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I shall try to comply with the wishes of my hon. friend. I was particularly interested, as I always am in a debate of this kind, in the remarks of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). He spoke of the very lofty ideals he and all of us should have in a debate of this kind. I found his remarks a little interesting compared to the practices of the members of the New Democratic Party, both here and elsewhere. He was rather critical of both the official opposition and the government, and made charges that perhaps they have tried to divide the farmer and the labourer in the past. He made no mention of the fact that particularly in Saskatchewan they have attempted for many years to divide the east from the west, and to bring about any other divisiveness they could put their hands on. It was interesting to hear the hon. member skate around the facts and try

to cover all the ground without really offending either side.
The hon. member did make one point when he said something to the effect that there is nothing new in the situation in which we find ourselves today. In that regard he is correct except that surely we, as parliamentarians and the people in this country, should have been able to learn something from the experiences of the various stoppages we have had to put up with through the years. I was very happy to hear of the settlement announced by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) tonight. Apparently the strike has been settled.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES
speechtext: What about the next one?

I believe there have been four or five such cases over the past few years. The hon. member who moved the motion said that there had been four cases in the past two or three years in which the Parliament of Canada had to intervene. subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   PUBLIC SERVICE EFFECT OF STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP ON GRAIN DELIVERIES
speechtext:
Yes, or should have. I should like to congratulate the President of the Treasury Board for the work he has done in bringing about this settlement. Collective bargaining is always a difficult process. Despite the fact that we have been involved in this for many years there is still much we have to learn about it. Collective bargaining is doubly difficult when the Government of Canada is the employer, particularly at a time when there is inflation in this country. Inflation certainly adds to the problems of both the workers and the employers, whether the employers be the government or other agencies.
As I have said, the President of the Treasury Board has obtained a settlement under the free collective bargaining process. I suppose the result of that process in this particular dispute might indicate to many people, both inside and outside this House, that the collective bargaining process is really working well. I say that would be an erroneous conclusion to draw in so far as at least these industrial disputes relate to the grain industry in this country. The collective bargaining process certainly has not served the Canadian grain industry well during the past few years.
There are about 160,000 to 170,000 farmers in western Canada, and many other people who are affected by the kind of disruption we have seen over the past six or eight months in the grain industry. These people have every respect for the right of the workers and employees to strike against their employers. They also appreciate the problems of the working man, whether he is working in the grain industry weighing grain in Vancouver or is loading boxcars on the prairies or anywhere else.
However, the question which must be asked sometime by the grain producer particularly, and by other Canadians whether or not they are directly involved in the production of grain, is when does the right of the worker come before the right of the producer to produce his product, put it on the market, obtain markets, and be
March 19, 1975

assured of future markets for his product? The farmer has a dozen and one things to contend with from the time he plants his crop until he gets it to market and receives a payment the amount of which he does not know. When does the right of the prairie farmer transcend the right in this case of 20 to 40 weighmen who have the right to strike? The farmer does not question this right.
I think this is one classic example, if we need any more, of the fact that we must immediately explore some better ways and means of resolving these disputes and differences before they reach the strike stage. The strike weapon where it directly involves only the employer and employee is very legitimate, and I certainly will defend that. Who knows, as someone said earlier, when we may have to be back here again in a week or two to deal with a similar situation in one of the many other possible disputes that could occur in the grain industry? I think we need to examine, explore and study very seriously some alternative methods to resolve these disputes before they get to the strike stage. Perhaps some special voluntary arbitration procedures could be implemented on a trial basis, as an example to try to see if we might be able to show the way in other industrial disputes.
Last weekend, at the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities Convention, western farmers attending the meeting said to me that they are prepared to support a national policy on energy where the taxpayers of Saskatchewan and Alberta, as the oil producing provinces, are receiving less than they would be if they were getting world prices for their resources. They are saying today that surely the rest of Canada should show them some consideration in trying to find a better solution to the disputes that have been so disruptive to the grain industry.

Madam Speaker, I will start from the beginning again after that slight interruption. I would like to say that the port of Churchill provides Manitoba with a unique distinction among the prairie provinces because of its access to the sea. The port has a fine harbour protected from the open sea. There are 3,065 feet of wharf with five deep sea berths and one coastal berth. The deep sea berths and turning basin at present are a maximum of 30 feet deep, that is at low tide, with tides running 11 to 15 feet. The major product moved out of the port of Churchill to date has been grain.
Western grain has been shipped from the port of Churchill since 1931, but the full capacity of that port has never really been tested. Since 1931, which is 44 years, the port of Churchill has never been affected by a strike. Let me just repeat what the hon. member for Assiniboia said. He said that he thought there ought to be a national conference or gathering to bring together the people concerned in all aspects of the grain trade.
I think we can expand that far beyond the grain trade in terms of labour relations. We can expand it into other areas of commerce and industry that are important to this country, and upon which we depend. I congratulate him for saying that, because the government that he supports, which has been in office since 1963, and which goes to the opposition for alternatives without producing any itself, has had the opportunity to take the kind of action he suggests, but not once has it done so.
The hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley also made a fine speech. He recognized the difficulty his own party has placed him in so far as his constituents and his province are concerned. In his eloquent way he made the same condemnation of lack of action by the government since it came to office in 1963.
In addition to speaking in the House of Commons for the record, I should also like these two members to go to caucus next Wednesday and speak to their colleagues in exactly the same terms. The hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo), I thought, made a very forceful speech, and perhaps put the situation best of all in terms of breadth when she talked about other industries. I should like her to go to the Liberal caucus next week and make the same speech. I should like her to make the absent members from the treasury benches tonight, and the 100 odd absent members of the government, listen to her. I assume that if they do not come to the House for important debates they must at least attend caucus, so I think those speeches should be made there as well.
I listened very carefully to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) who spoke tonight, and waited for some of the alternatives which they have asked of the opposition. But why do they not produce alternatives during the course of the debate? The people of Canada gave this government a mandate on July 8. I do not begrudge it the mandate, though I wish it were otherwise. But they did not give the government a mandate to ask the opposition what to do about the problems of this country; the people of Canada were looking to the government to lead and to offer alternatives; they looked to the government to heal the wounds, to give leadership and to inspire Canadians.
Unfortunately the government has a majority but is in relative shambles. If there is one place where we are going to witness lack of leadership in Canada in 1975 and 1976, it is in the very vexing field of employer-employee relations.
I do not want to speak about the general labour market, but I do want to say something about the public service of this country. I respect the right to strike, though I hope it will always be used in a responsible way. But I also think we should look to the national interest from time to time and, as the President of the Treasury Board said, there is a

time for judgment. He said that in his opinion the time for judgment with respect to the grain trade had not come.
I say to him that he was wrong, that he exercised that judgment improperly. That is not to say that the issue is not important. The farmers and the people who depend on the grain trade decided a long time ago that the matter was in the national interest.
The minister asked for alternatives, and I should like to tell him about what I would like to see in regard to public service bargaining. I should like to see a widening of bargaining rights in this country, of the fields in which public servants can bargain, and of the matters about which they can bargain. It is important to establish, or perhaps re-establish, good faith in the public service between employers and employees. That was the purpose of the Finkelman report, but I do not think that is in existence. If the government members of that commission were to move in that direction, then I think we would be opening the door to the beginning of industrial peace and trust in this country.
The second thing we ought to do is re-establish the pay research bureau. It was a very good thing and it could take an independent look at pay structures and the whole matter of comparability. All the evidence placed before that bureau ought to be laid on the table so that all parties, including the public, could see what the case is. This is not the case now. If anything came out of the Finkelman report, it is the fact that this has not been done but ought to be done.
I think we have to take a hard look at the whole concept of industrial democracy in the private sector so that trust can be built up and perhaps transcend itself-if that is the correct phrase-into the public sector. We ought to strive for that in the committee. Government members, particularly, ought not to limit the debate, limit the thrust of that committee or dampen down the areas we can discuss but should, rather, widen them so we can build into the public service side the real, consultative procedures which are not now there. The rudiments are there, but in terms of good, sound consultative procedures they are not there.
We ought to explore the whole question of a public interest disputes commission. Part of the problem in respect of labour relations in Canada, in the public or private sector, is that there is no machinery anywhere to examine a contract while it is in force or to deal with problems that arise from time to time while a contract is running and isolate the problems before the contract expires. In this way negotiation would be limited and the beds sores that come during a period of conflict would be eliminated. We need that kind of consultative procedure in this country. We also need bargaining procedures in both the public and private sectors. We need bargaining procedures that are swift and responsive so the frustrations that come in the course of time do not build up and attitudes do not harden. The minister asked for some suggestions, and those are a few I offer in the short time I have to deal with this matter.
I am a little concerned about what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) has said. I thought one aspect of his speech set a very high tone in respect of what we look for

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the most perplexing things to try to figure out in this House is how to understand a Liberal government. Their members get up in the House and suggest that members of the opposition complain but never come up with any suggestions. Just now, when the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) made a number of suggestions, hon. members said they were not interested in hearing them-and I think that describes the attitude of hon. members opposite tonight.
At this hour, 20 minutes after one o'clock in the morning, I think it is interesting to point out that the Liberals said this issue is not in the national interest. I think if we are to be positive and constructive in respect of the government we have to concede that it believes it is not in the national interest. It would seem that the government does believes this because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) never once showed up for this debate. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) came for his speech and then left. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) did not remain here except for a few minutes. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was never here once.
Tonight I will document some information to show that this is a very important issue in terms of the national interest. Throughout the debates in recent days we have heard that collective bargaining is a right. I will not deny that is so. However, we also must bear in mind that this society has no such a thing as rights in isolation. A right is a concept that is co-related and interwoven with responsibility.
When we look at the broad spectrum of our society we note that many aspects to which we claim rights also have clearly defined responsibilities. First, if we have the right to drive a car we have the responsibility to be licensed and the responsibility to drive on the correct side of the road. We have the right to breathe air; but have the responsibility not to pollute it. But let us look at what the Liberals have been telling us. They speak about the right to strike regardless of whether or not any responsibility is being shown. Let me give an example. In answer to a question by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) the Prime Minister replied in part:
The answer really lies at which point the public interest becomes overwhelming and should overwhelm the basic democratic right to strike which has been given by parliament to the workers of this nation.
Then on March 18, as recorded at page 4195 of Hansard, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver South, the President of the Treasury Board replied in part as follows:

March 19, 1975
Grain Shipments
Mr. Speaker, I said previously and I will repeat that those employees have the right to strike, and we respect that right to strike. The House has not indicated to me that we should withdraw the right to strike.
There is no mention of a parallel set of responsibilities. Then at page 4199 of Hansard for March 18, in reply to a question of mine, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) said:
This is a dispute situation. In a dispute situation such as this, we could not get into the question of assessing liability on innocent third parties. That is an inevitable result when you have the right to strike.
One would gather from the Minister of Labour that damage irrespective of amount is simply a part of labour-management negotiations. When the leader of this party asked the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp) a question on March 7, 1975, as recorded at page 3879 of Hansard, he replied:
It is the law of this country that people do have the right to strike.
As a thesis to my case I wish to point out that there are no rights in this country without parallel sets of responsibilities. We might refer to the Canadian Bill of Rights which lays down the basic rights for people. It talks about rights such as freedom of speech, freedom of religion and freedom of the press. We know in fact that none of those rights exist without responsibilities. In the second paragraph of the Canadian Bill of Rights we find this:
Affirming also that men and institutions remain free only when freedom is founded upon respect for moral and spiritual values and the rule of law;
When we take a look at the question of spiritual and moral laws I challenge this government, when the largest ship ever to go to the port of Vancouver is stranded at that port waiting to take grain destined for Bangladesh, to show where its sense of moral and spiritual law is.
I challenge members of the government to come forward and say what their mores are when they say this is not in the national interest. They take this position despite the fact that 12,000 people a day are dying of starvation or malnutrition. One must ask vhere is the moral obligation of this government when only 40 people can hold up the grain industry. Yet they have the audacity to talk about the rights of labour and management. Have we once heard these members opposite talk about the result in respect of third parties? Who is looking after the farmers who, in every instance, end up paying at least part of the shot and who, by their very nature, are prevented from being able to strike in order to retain some of the benefits for themselves?
This evening we heard a speech by the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. All I could conclude when the minister finished his speech was that I had never witnessed a greater example of an abortion created on the western farmers than by the Minister of Justice. The President of the Treasury Board referred to this debate tonight as a little strike. I dare him to go to the constituencies of western Canada and refer to this as a little strike.
I think the Liberal Party could be well known as an animal called the cheeta in respect of the western farm people because members of that party have shown their callousness in respect of this issue where it concerns the people who are in need of the production we can produce. I should like to document how serious the situation has

been to the prairie farmer and how insensitive the present government has been. While I hear echoes from the other side I shall document how serious this is.
The government has cheated the farmer for the last couple of years in relation to the port of Vancouver. Let us deal first from the start of the crop year commencing with the week of July 28 to August 3, 1974. At that time we had the west coast grain handlers' strike which started on May 19, 1974. Let us go to the second week, the week of August 4 to August 10. The west coast grain handlers' strike continued and the Great Lakes lake operators strike started on August 8, 1974. In that same week there was a CNR derailment and the Albreda sub-line was closed on August 6.
Let us go to the week of August 11 to August 17. The west coast grain handlers' strike is on. The Great Lake operators strike continues, and there is another train derailment of the CNR at mile 25.1 at the Yale substation.
Let us move on to the fourth week of the crop year from August 18 to 24. The labour strike of the west coast grain handlers is continuing under work to rule. The Great Lake operators strike continues, and there is a derailment of trains on the CPR at mile 13.4, Mountain substation. The main line was closed on August 18. Let us move on to the fifth week of the crop year. The west coast grain handlers strike is still in effect. The Great Lake operators strike continues, and there are two more derailments, one on the CNR and one on the CPR.
Let us now consider the sixth week from September 1 to
7.	Here again we have the west coast grain handlers strike, the Great Lake operators strike, and another derailment of CPR on mile 38.3 at Mountain substation on September 1, 1974. Let us go on to the seventh week of the crop year from September 8 to 14. We have the west coast grain handlers strike continuing, the Great Lakes operators strike continuing, and three train derailments, the CNR derailment at mile 120.5 at the Ashcroft substation, the CNR derailment at mile 64.6 at the Fraser substation, and the CNR derailment at mile 64.6 at the Fraser substation at Prince Rupert.
Now let us review the eighth week of the crop year from September 15 to 21. The west coast grain handlers strike continues, the Great Lakes operators strike continues. That takes us to the ninth week of the crop year from September 22 to 28 when the west coast grain handlers strike continues, and the Great Lakes operators strike continues. Let us move on to the tenth week from September 29 to October 5 when the west coast handlers strike continues, the Great Lakes operators strike continues and there are two derailments, the CNR derailment at mile 38.4 at the Skeena substation at Prince Rupert and the CPR derailment at mile 104.3 at Mountain substation.
In the eleventh week of the crop year the west coast grain handlers strike ended on October 10, 1974. Then we move on to the twelfth and thirteenth weeks and, whoopee poo, there are two whole weeks in which all the unions are working and, miraculously, not a single derailment takes place.
But lest the Grits become too happy, let us move on to the fourteenth week, from October 27 to November 2,

when the west coast grain inspectors did not report to work, at Thunder Bay the government inspectors did not report to work either, and there was a derailment of the CNR at mile 81.1 at the Albreda substation. In the fifteenth week all unions were working.
In the sixteenth week again all unions were working and, lest the Grits become too happy let us remind them that a derailment of the CPR took place in that week. However, that is the end of the joy, and certainly the Liberals deserve no credit for it because on the seventeenth week from November 17 to 23 the west coast, Thunder Bay and government grain inspectors strike is in effect. Also, the British Columbia railroad shop craft strike is on, there is a CPR derailment at mile 68.9 at the Windermere substation, a CPR derailment at mile 105.6 at the Cascade substation, and a CPR derailment at the Rossland substation which was closed on November 25.
Let us move on to the eighteenth week of the crop year from November 24 to 30. The west coast and Thunder Bay government grain inspectors strike is on. The west coast and interior government grain inspectors returned to work at 12 noon on December 5, 1974, and the Thunder Bay government inspectors returned to work on December 5, 1974. We now have tremendous joy so far as the Liberals are concerned, despite the fact that they had nothing to do with it. There were three weeks in which all unions were working.
This is a terrible history of strikes and derailments all of which effect the farmer. Then, on the twenty-fourth week from January 5 to 11, the British Columbia railroad shop craft returned to work, but there is a derailment of the CPR at Revelstoke, B.C. We find that when we consider the thirty-six weeks, including the present week, that in almost none of that time was there any smooth delivery of grain in this country.
It is about time that we laid the record straight and began to understand what farming is. Farming is not a life style, it is not a way of life. Farming is the production of food, the ms>st essential of industries, the most essential of all businesses. Yet, despite the fact that food is required to maintain life, the government has not done anything constructive to encourage the shipping of grain to market at a time when, if we could hypothetically distribute food around the world, we would not have enough protein to go around. The situation is extremely critical, and it is high time that we put all our efforts into attempting to get grain to market faster.
We heard the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campag-nolo) say tonight that farmers are not the only Canadians, and she challenged the prairie farmers' representatives here in parliament not to make such an issue about farm people. I also concede that farmers are not the only people, but I darn well claim that they are people and their rights are at least equal to those of other people. When we take a look at what has been happening in the grain movement, starting in May of last year, we find that in total there have only been eleven weeks of free movement of grain in this country. I say that there is not another industry in Canada which could operate year after year under the insensitive kind of policies which the government sets with regard to the agricultural industry.
Grain Shipments
It is important to set the record straight. The strikes that were taking place recently were supposedly rotating strikes. Yet, what did we witness on the west coast at the port of Vancouver? The only strikes that were continuous and not being rotated were those that were affecting the grain industry. Labour organizations were once again putting on the pressure where they knew it hurts. I think it is time we heard not just speeches from the government in which it talks about the right to strike but speeches about the rights of all Canadians, whether they be farmers, labour organizations or people in management. All rights go with responsibilities, and rights and responsibilities should not be separated. A right is something that is earned. Those who practice rights, irrespective of whether or not people die as a result, and irrespective of whether or not agriculture survives, should expect those rights to be challenged.
The question is whether or not we should be allowed to practice the right to strike when the national interest is at stake. What we hear from the Prime Minister, the Minister of Labour, and the President of the Treasury Board is that despite the fact that agriculture has been disrupted for almost two solid years, this is not a national issue.
I know of no hypocrisy greater than singling out within a nation a group of people, who are important both in terms of numbers and in what they produce, and then turn a blind eye to them and say that we do not care about their interests because we are protecting the interests of labour and management. It is high time that we lent full consideration to the damage inflicted upon innocent third parties.
I have made the following statement in this House before, and I will make it again tonight, that I believe there are legal grounds for farm organizations in this country to sue with regard to demurrage charges laid upon them due to strikes this past year at the port of Vancouver. I know of no business principle which allows two parties to negotiate and incur an expense and then charge that expense to a third party, yet that is what has happened at the port of Vancouver. We witnessed labour and management causing ships to be held up in port incurring an expense of at least $17 million-and there are estimates that it may be well over $50 million-and the full amount will be borne by the western Canadian farmer.
I think that that is such a shame that it should be tested in our courts because there are no precedents whereby two parties can incur an expense and charge that expense to a third party. I think that anyone who is closely observing the labour-management disputes is witnessing many kinds of illegal activity. It is on that basis that I think there is still a tremendous amount to be done in terms of setting up programs to alleviate these labour disputes which are so drastically affecting prairie farmers and subsequently our world markets.
There have been only two occasions since August of 1973 when vessels have not been waiting to load in Vancouver, and those two occasions amounted to only 18 working days. As of March 10 of this year, 30 vessels have been waiting and 15,000 boxcars from the west are bunched up at the port of Vancouver, and so we see, Mr. Speaker-

speechtext:
I have never seen a group of people who cared so little for the public as the treasury benches of the Liberal government in 1975. They are a disgrace to the democratic system by any measurement which might be applied, and hon. members opposite, who sit there like a bunch of idle servants, should certainly tell them where they stand tomorrow. They have abused the very principles which are the responsibility of elected democratic representatives, particularly those who are willing to assume by appointment the responsibility for a cabinet position.
Let us consider the movement of grain in the Dominion of Canada in the last three years. Did hon. members opposite know that in the first quarter of 1972 we did not move as much grain as we did in the first quarter of 1971? Did they know that in the second quarter of 1972 we did not move as much grain as we did in the first quarter of 1971? Did they know that in the third quarter of 1972 we moved 15 million bushels less than in the third quarter of 1971? I could go on. In the fourth quarter of 1972 we did pretty well. There was good shipment. But let us go back again to 1973. The market was picking up, and there was a demand. We find that in the first quarter of 1973 we did not ship as much as we did in the first quarter of 1971. In the second quarter of 1973 we did not ship as much as we did in 1971. In the third quarter of 1973 we did not do as well as well as we did in 1971. The first three quarters of 1974 were the worst of all.
Any Liberal member who has been responsible enough to get himself elected to the House of Commons must share some of the responsibility, whether he sits on the backbenches or the frontbenches, for a deplorable state of transportation, labour problems, and disorganization which this government has perpetrated in the name of a majority or a minority government.
